Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of pressing and considerable importance. In view of major energy, environmental and conservation gains through recycling of many products, including iron, copper, aluminium and paper, and in view of the recent comments by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) regarding his appreciation of the opportunities, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek):
That the government integrate the already considerable recycling industries into a development and industrial strategy for Canada, and provide direct and indirect encouragement to the Canadian Association of Recycling Industries.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT BORROWING COSTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in view of the fact that commercial borrowers can borrow on commercial paper in the United States at 15 per cent, or borrow on bankers' acceptances for 90 days at 16.5 per cent, that international corporations can borrow on the Euro-dollar at approximately 17.5 per cent, that the American government can borrow its 90-day treasury bill money at 14.3 per cent, and in view of the fact that this government today paid 18.83 per cent to borrow its 90-day money, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett):
That the government immediately constitute a special committee of this House to inquire as to why the Government of Canada pays significantly more to borrow money than commercial corporations pay in the United States, than multinational corporations pay on the world market and the United States government pays on its treasury bills, and that this House does censor this government for deliberately maintaining a high interest rate policy in Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF SMALL BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT BOND PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance has responded to questions in a way which implies that he understands the economic crisis which primary Canadian producers are facing now, small businessmen and farmers. He says he recognizes the crisis. He is also aware of the offer this side of the House has made for a one day's extended debate, or whatever is required, to allow expansion of the small business development bond to include operating capital and venture financing, and also to include unincorporated businesses.
I wonder if the Minister of Finance can tell the House and the Canadian people whether he intends to make the announcement he has discussed, or whether we are forced to go through the summer without knowing before the end of this session of Parliament whether or not this will be an opportunity to which small businessmen and farmers can look forward.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member has referred to the small business development bond which, in its present operation, is of very substantial benefit to small busi-
Oral Questions
ness. As I have indicated previously in the House, the Canadian banks have dedicated about $750 million for the use of the small business development bond already, and I am told by the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism that when all the institutions together are added up, the total amount dedicated to the small business bond is about $2 billion. That is a very substantial source of funding at about half the market rates for small businesses intending to engage in expansion and modernization.
There is, in addition, a provision in the bond by which funds can be made available to small businesses in financial difficulty. As I have indicated in the House previously, we have had discussions with the chartered banks to make it possible that wider use be made of this particular aspect of the bond in order to help small businesses in refinancing difficulties. In the present circumstances the small business development bond is an extremely useful and effective instrument, and in that light it is not my intention, for example, to recommend its extension to unincorporated businesses because of almost impossible administrative problems which would be involved.

Madam Speaker, I am familiar with some of the figures the minister has mentioned in terms of the financing of the bond and in terms of the amounts of money which have been dedicated by the institutions. The point I would really like to make in my supplementary question is the impact there is on primary producers because of the high interest rate policy and the fact that the small business development bond as it stands now does not address that, and that the primary producers cannot continue to produce with interest rates of 20 per cent to 23 per cent. They cannot continue to stay in business.
The minister is well aware of the number of bankruptcies. He is well aware of the impact on the total economy. There must be an extension of that program. There must be a provision for opening that up to relieve the financial pressure on agricultural producers and small businessmen of the country. Because of the impact there is now and the impact there will be on the total economy, people who were initially hurt are now becoming tremendously aggressive and angry.
The minister must look at some other measure. If he does not wish to use that measure, is there any other specific measure the minister has in mind which he will introduce before this session of Parliament ends so that these people have something to which they may look forward?

subsubtopic: METRIC CONVERSION OF "CALORIE"
speechtext:
In so far as Metric Commission Canada is concerned:
1.	The Weights and Measures Act of 1971 specifies the International System of Units (SI) as the latest evolution of the metric system to be legal in Canada. The calorie and the erg are obsolete metric units which, not being coherent, in the case of the calorie, nor a preferred sub-multiple, in the case of the erg, are not used with International System of Units (SI). (Source-CSA "Canada Metric Practice Guide" 1979 Edition). The joule and its preferred decimal multiples and submultiples will replace both the calorie and the erg. The kilojoule is equivalent to one thousand joules.
Most everyone is familiar with the SI unit of power, the watt, and the expenditure of energy at the rate of one joule per second produces a power of one watt. The energy consumed by a 100 W light bulb is 100 J/s (joules per second), and if one leaves a 100 W light bulb burning for one hour the energy consumption is 360,000 J or 360 KJ (kilojoules). Other ways of expressing this are obviously 100 W.h (watt hours) equals 360 KJ (kilojoules) or 1 W.h equals 3.6 KJ.
The use of the kilojoule was recommended for the human diet by the Intersectorial Committee on the Adoption of the Kilojoule in its 1975 report and again in its revised 1980 report. This is a committee of Metric Commission Canada under the Health and Welfare Sector. It is made up of
Order Paper Questions
volunteer members representing diverse groups such as: Canadian Medical Association, Canadian Dietetic Association, Canadian Grocery Products Manufacturers Association, Consumers' Association of Canada, and the Sports Federation of Canada.
2.	The benefits of adopting the joule parallel those of adopting the International System of Units, including rationalization of energy terms and simplification of energy calculations.
(a)	Rationalization
The use of the joule will promote consistency, rationalizing the many units now used for energy into a single unit. This one unit, the joule, will replace the several calorie terms such as large calorie, kilocalorie, thermo-chemical calorie, cal 15, IT calorie, in addition to replacing other energy terms such as British Thermal Unit and therm.
(b)	Simplification
Various types of energy are interconvertible. Because the joule will be the sole unit used to describe energy, time and money will be saved by reducing the number of calculations required in converting among energy units. Only one energy unit will need to be taught, thus saving time in the educational process. It is the internationally accepted SI unit for energy.
Potential benefits of this are: it will facilitate tracing of convertible energy in the ecological cycle; facilitate economic studies for the efficient convertibility of energy; simplify comparison of data among scientific disciplines; and facilitate cost-benefit analyses of energy required for crop production versus energy released by metabolization of crops produced.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58(10)-ALLEGED FAILURE TO BRING BEFORE PARLIAMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
ALLOTTED DAY S O. 58(10)-ALLEGED FAILURE TO BRING BEFORE PARLIAMENT ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for failing to bring before Parliament effective economic policies to deal with the present economic crisis and end the disastrous interest rate squeeze on the small business, industrial and agricultural sectors.
He said: Madam Speaker, this motion is put forward on our final opposition day of this session at a time when there has been criticism of this party in terms of the motions we have brought forward previously, and also at a time when there is a question in terms of government inaction in addressing the economic difficulties faced by Canada today.
1 would like to restate the motion we put forward because 1 think it is really at the heart of the difficulties in terms of the government's viewpoint and what needs to be done:
That this House condemns the government for failing to bring before Parliament effective economic policies to deal with the present economic crisis and end the disastrous interest rate squeeze on the small business, industrial and agricultural sectors.
That is a fairly strongly worded motion, Mr. Speaker. The word "condemn" is there, a word I think none of us likes to use in normal conversation, particularly when addressing the Government of Canada. However, it is an appropriate word because the inaction of the government in addressing what is truly an economic crisis threatens in the long term to put us in a position where economic recovery will be impossible. In the short term it addresses the issue of what will happen to the primary producers of this country.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has heard all this before. The difficulty is that he is not addressing the problem. He answered some questions today in a way that really slips through and slides around the issue and difficulties being faced by producers, small businessmen and the people of Canada who are facing the brunt of these economic policies.
Whatever the minister has said so far, the bottom line of the whole issue is that what he is doing is not working. If he argues that his high interest rate policy is to reduce consumer spending, he makes the case very well today that the pressure for loans on the banks is as high as ever. The fact is that we are facing continuously high interest rates which have not decreased in the face of government policy over the past six or nine months, ever since, in fact, the government took power. The situation is not improving; rather it is deteriorating.
One of the main problems faced by the government, and the Minister of Finance addressed this very directly in some of his comments today, is that the high interest rate policy by itself is not the single problem. There is no question about that. It indeed happens to be the biggest single problem faced by producers, by entrepreneurs who would like to start a business, or small businessmen who have an opportunity to expand but cannot because they cannot face the interest rate charges. He talked about fertilizer in the agriculture industry.
The Minister of Finance just spoke proudly of Bill C-57. He has to know that in that bill he imposes a 30-cent tax which affects the cost of fertilizer, the cost of home heating for numerous Canadians, that in fact affects our ability to export because exports of natural gas to the United States are down 25 per cent. Minimum quantities of gas are being taken because American consumers do not want to face that additional charge and they are now looking to their own supplies. So instead of taking the maximum amount which would return revenue to the government, they take minimum amounts, which again reduces government revenue. Farmers must face the higher fertilizer costs in combination with the other pressures they have. Home owners and people who must pay heating bills have to face these higher costs. So it is in fact a combination of effects as a result of the government's total economic policy which has led us to the crisis we are now facing.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, individual Canadians are proud people. They do not want to face financial losses such that they have to declare bankruptcy. They do not want to suffer what they consider to be the shame in their own minds, if not in others, of incurring the losses and failure identified by the statistics we call bankruptcies. That is why those statistics do not tell the story about Canadians who withdraw from or do not enter into business activities or farming. They do not tell about the people who quietly go their way without complaint because they have pride, a pride which we should try and foster.
It is a little like the farmer I talked to last night who has farmed for his entire life and has a son who would like to farm. He would like to help him but he is faced with a situation now, with interest rates being the single most significant economic
Economic Policies
factor, where he has sold his farm and will sell the rest of his property and withdraw completely from agriculture because he sees no future in it. That person is representative of the over 1,000 people in Ontario who withdraw from agriculture each year.
The Minister of Finance spoke about the strength of the agricultural community. Indeed, that is true. There are 700,000 people in Ontario alone who are either directly or indirectly affected by and depend on agriculture for their livelihood. That figure is vulnerable today because that community is vulnerable as a result of the combination of effects, with interest rates being the most important.
Last fall businessmen responded to a survey by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. On questions regarding the effects of high interest rates on their particular businesses, 55 per cent of them responded by showing their profits were in fact reduced as a direct consequence of these rates. That is a sector of our economy, Mr. Speaker, which accounts for somewhere near 60 per cent of employment. Those people are vulnerable. They face the same kind of pressure. Indeed, they are the same kind of people who do not want to face bankruptcy and who will withdraw, if they can, quietly and proudly in order to avoid the shame of bankruptcy. The number of those people is the number which is really important, and the number of those people will be quadrupled by the fall of this year.
The question which must come up is wherein the responsibility lies for the present crisis. We know from the statistics of 1980 that consumer spending figures are fantastic. The amount of money Canadian consumers have spent on consumer goods is somewhere around $167 billion. In one way or another the people of Canada are entrapped in a situation which has left them as individual consumers at a point where they have a habit of spending perhaps more than they should and have a credit habit which has been fostered over years of affluence.
The government has been in power now for 16 years with the exception of nine months. The government itself must set an example. In looking at the example the government has set for them, these people must ask themselves these serious questions: Where is the government coming from; what is it saying; what is it doing? The government has campaigned and repeatedly indicated the effort it has made to reduce its deficits and the effort it must make to reduce its spending. The bottom line is what the government is actually doing in contrast to what it is saying or the example it would like to set for Canadians. We know that we are spending well over $60 billion this year and that the deficit has risen to $14 billion. This is the kind of example Canadians have come to look to; it is the kind of model they have to follow in their own personal lives. This is one of the critical reasons why there is great difficulty in looking at a resolution to this problem.
The other aspect is the banks. Are the banks the ones to blame? What is happening with the banks? If we look at some

June 26, 1981
Economic Policies
of their statistics and quarterly figures, we will see some amazing results in terms of operating profits and revenues. In the case of one bank, in the first quarter of 1981 its operating profit was $211 million. In the second quarter of 1981 the profits rose by a factor of four to $1,140 million. Not all banks have followed the same dramatic increase; there have been some changes.
The minister was talking about the small business development bond this afternoon. He discussed the amount of money which was put into the small business development bond. In fact, it is somewhere around $700 million and it could be about $2 billion, if things keep going the same way, by the end of 1981. Those figures have not really influenced the profits of banks. In that case they will not influence the taxation aspect of the banking system. The banks have indeed done well. There is no question that it is costing them more money to borrow and there is a balance somewhere. The banks have been part of the scheme. Their rates have been usurious. They have been criticized. In fact they are the focal point of individuals faced with bearing the brunt of high interest rates. They are part of the system, and the bottom line of the system is the government which needs to provide leadership but has provided no example at all.
The government's example is so ingrained and so much a part of the system that there will have to be a dramatic reversal in a number of areas in order for there to be any improvement. The specialization which occurs in the different branches of government is one of the key issues. These are broad issues which will not provide us with the answers today, but they are worth mentioning because they are important.
Let us compare the people in the Department of Finance with those in the Department of Agriculture and in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. These people are focused in their own territory. They have become highly specialized in one area. They have no sense of the integration which is required or of the ripple effects of their actions and directions in a number of areas. These people are well qualified. They have come up through a system which has perpetuated very understandably their own self-interest. They have a position, they have a territory. Unfortunately the necessary overview for economic survival and enhancement of the whole system is not there. It is somewhat like a specialist in pediatrics who deals with infants. He is topnotch in his own area, but he wonders why the mother of his patient who is on welfare goes out and becomes pregnant again; perhaps he will treat another child with the same congenital disease.
The problem is that there is no one focusing and putting together the different aspects. There is no one who has a feeling for it. As capable and well-intentioned as is the Minister of Finance, he does not have a grasp of what is really happening in terms of the energy future, the agricultural aspects of the economy, or some important things which are necessary for economic recovery. The integration of all those matters is not there.
The Minister of Finance likes to discuss the international aspects or the impact of such things as interest rates in the
United States upon the Canadian scene. It has been mentioned many times before but it needs to be mentioned again that not only do we have a unique situation in Canada in terms of opportunities, distances, and a range of important elements but we have a system of government which has developed over a period of time.
Within that system we have developed a particular rationale for economic and monetary policies which does not take into account any of the other things happening in the United States at the present time, such as the bill before Congress to reduce taxation by $35 billion. The Americans brought in bills which deregulated the oil and gas industry to allow the private sector to thrive, to do the things which needed to be done in terms of exploration and development, and to do everything necessary for their energy future to be as secure as possible. Canada has not dealt with these matters in the same way. This is not good. It is really like trying to avoid the real issue by saying, "Yes, interest rates have an impact on our system and what we do in Canada with interest rates". But we cannot do this in isolation. If we look upon the Americans as an example of what to do, we should look at what they are doing in other areas as well to regenerate their economy. Perhaps we just hope to slide along with them in the event they are successful.
My final point concerns government priorities. A moment ago I mentioned the criticism that we on this side of the House have endured because we chose to use one allotted day to consider a moral issue. The day after, the government chose to introduce a bill on hijacking. The government has numerous opportunities, endless days, wherein it can introduce any legislation it wants. We on this side of the House would be more than pleased to co-operate and to deal with the serious economic issues with which the country is faced rather than the peripheral issues that are important in many ways but have no real effect upon the economic situation of Canada.
What are the results of this interest rate policy which we now have in this country? I think that the most succinct expression of this comes from a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) from the Canadian Institute for Economic Policy, which I would like to read. I am sure that the Minister of Finance has read this letter. There are six points in it. These points state, in terms of what I consider to be a very credible body, the effects of the interest rate policy. I would simply like to describe them now. First:
They have slowed down the rate of growth in the economy with the result that we have higher levels of unemployment than should be permitted.
That unemployment level is now well over a million and may be 1.25 million.
The cost of unemployment, the under-utilization of our human resources, can be measured in economic terms. But the social cost represented by the frustration of those who cannot find jobs, and sometimes the broken homes that are the result, are no less real even though they cannot be measured statistically. Moreover, a sluggish economy means that government revenues are depressed and thus government deficits are considerably higher than they should be.
I am sure that the Minister of Finance has heard of the Lefler Curve, the disincentive in terms of taxation and the
June 26, 1981

experiences which have been gained in other countries, and the disincentive for individuals, for entrepreneurs and for business to engage in business activities because of the taxation rate. I think that is the emphasis of the first point which this report has brought forward. Second:
Small and medium-sized businesses-most of which are Canadian owned- tend to borrow heavily from the banks for their capital requirements. As interest rates have gone up, more of these businesses have been driven into bankruptcy. The number of bankruptcies in March 1981 was 29 per cent higher than for the comparable month a year ago. With interest rates now payable by small businesses of 20 per cent or even higher, more bankruptcies can be expected.
The minister, in answer to questions earlier, responded by saying that the total number was not bad. While he is in the House, I would like to say that, in fact, the absolute numbers are not that great when one looks at Canada as a nation. However, when one talks about those numbers, one is really not talking about the impact that these interest rates are having because of the number of Canadians who voluntarily withdraw, first of all, from their businesses and their enterprises, whether it is farming, tourism or whatever. It really goes beyond that, because at some point in time some of those people who have been severely affected even tend to withdraw from our system and lose confidence in it.
Third:
High interest rates discourage all business enterprises, both large and small, from investing in new plant and equipment. The exact opposite is needed in the interests of improved productivity.
Fourth:
High interest rates have increased costs all through the economy and, therefore, are themselves inflationary.
This is another principle which the Minister of Finance continues to deny, will not accept and will not face:
In particular, they have added substantially to the cost of housing. This makes it very difficult, if not impossible, for young people starting life to purchase a home of their own, which is still the dream of most Canadians.
Fifth:
High mortgage rates are causing considerable difficulties for home owners and for some farmers. Some have lost their homes as a result.
Finally, sixth:
The Bank's continued efforts to encourage an inflow of capital, by keeping interest rates high, has resulted in a substantial increase in our foreign debt. And the carrying charges on this debt have added to the deficit on current account in our balance of payments.
Those are the six consequences of the high interest rate policy of the government. I think they are well stated. They give a broad picture of what is happening because of the government's policy.
One of the critical issues which comes as a consequence of decreased business activity is a dependency on government to seek revenues in other areas. This is part of the disastrous cycle in which we now find ourselves in Canada. It is part of the rationale and the motivation for many of the measures which have been brought forward in bills such as Bill C-57.
The effects caused because the government wants to increase its revenue have strained the fibre of our national unity to almost the breaking point in many regions of our
Economic Policies
country. The issues are really premised on two things. They are premised on a question of central federal control which in many ways I would support, and I think it is appropriate; but they are also premised on the basis of government needing revenue because its other policies demand it. It does not invest or manage the economic affairs of the nation in a proper way. Therefore, it requires these revenues which, in themselves, defeat the purpose by decreasing activity in a number of areas.
Mention was made of the inflationary aspect of an ad valorem tax. This is unfortunate type of tax. Any ad valorem tax is unfortunate. However, it is unfortunate in the sense that, in itself; it again adds to inflationary pressure. It gives an example to everyone of the kinds of things which the government is going to do to maintain a revenue base when, indeed, the government should be trying to develop a tax base from a healthy economy instead.
I think there is no question that the only way we can achieve any resolution here is through economic leadership which must be provided by government. The banks will not do it. Individuals are now caught in circumstances where most of them really do not have an opportunity. Some larger corporations which have a considerable amount of equity may find some ways. However, in many cases those people are using a tax system which certainly will not provide increased revenue to the government in the short term, but they are avoiding taxes by doing things which larger institutions and corporations can do. In the end result, there might be a final concentration of power into larger corporations, chain stores and the sectors which can survive and withstand the pressures of the government's policies, or the government itself might expand and continue to have to try to provide support and relief measures for those people who have been disadvantaged and, in fact, thrown out of work by the policies which the government itself has created. People demand from the government and, in fact, need from the government the welfare support which is the only answer for their own personal survival.
However, the only way we can get recovery is through leadership from the government on an economic policy which will face, in terms of the productive sector, the needs it has in terms of borrowing costs, other advantages, the taxation system and deregulation and decontrol of the many aspects which are frustrating the production of many materials, including agriculture. There was an estimation that by simply deregulating, by simply taking away the massive controls and regulations which impose themselves upon the agricultural sector, the agricultural community, the primary producer, would save $1 billion a year in Canada.
There were a number of questions on the small business development bond earlier in the day. While the minister is now here, I would like to spend a moment on the small business development bond. At this time, according to the available figures, we have a diversion of funds through bank profits and other institutional profits of somewhere in excess of $700 million and calculations which bring us to $2 billion by the end of this year. Those funds are directed into specific areas, to specific groups which are able to qualify for them if, in fact,

June 26, 1981
Economic Policies
those institutions are prepared to provide that funding within their own economic situation.
The amount of money which will be diverted into that bonding mechanism by individual banks varies from bank to bank. There are some banks which have notably used that system well and have promoted and advanced it. There are many other banks, particularly as one goes away from the larger branches of those banks, which, first of all, do not have a clue about the terms of reference, which is partly their fault and, I suggest, partly the government's fault. However, one finds that at the small branch level individual managers are not familiar with all of the provisions of those bonds, and this has, in fact, been a major difficulty for local people in taking advantage of them. There is no question about this. It is a real fault in the system. If it is, in fact, going to function in a way which will help primary producers and small businessmen, those banks simply must be better informed. They must understand the issues and the opportunities better. They must be able to communicate clearly and succinctly in informing people whether their cases might be applicable to the bonds.
The minister also mentioned the question of being able to divert funds in certain cases to operating capital and to allow people to use these funds for other than new expansion in cases where there is economic difficulty. But the difficulty is with the limitation imposed. The bank is required not to lend that individual or incorporated business any further funds. That is a stranglehold and something which makes it impossible for any movement within a certain economic situation any individual farmer or small businessman might have.
The minister talked about the bureaucracy and the difficulties in administration. An application came to the department four months ago. The minister knows that these applications have to be considered on a case by case basis. As an example, four months ago an application was made on the part of a unit which was economically viable on the basis of being able to qualify for this bond. Today that unit is frustrated and is in more economic difficulty because of the interest rate charges. The company is now looking at selling out completely.
This sort of thing happens partly because of lack of familiarity and partly because of the hesitancy of the individual banks to use the mechanism. The banks feel vulnerable because of repercussions if the taxation department tells them the loan was not justifiable in the first place. The banks are concerned about their own situation a year or so down the road in the event that the taxation department comes back to tell them it was not the right thing to do. If we are going to use this mechanism, we should address it. It should be clearly stated and clearly identified and made to function in a way which would expedite the provisions so the people who could qualify would qualify. That is the very least the government can do right now. That requires an administrative change. It is something that is sitting waiting to be done right now, and it should be done quickly.
The other point which the minister made concerned the agricultural community. He said that the agricultural community might expect the minister would look to either unincorporated farms or incorporated farms. I was not clear just how he stated it.

He mentioned that there might be a provision within the bond to allow a special opportunity outside of this failure situation. Perhaps he could clarify that point.

Incorporated would present a difficulty for many farmers, but it can be overcome.
In conclusion, the time-frame is critical and important because it will end with this session of Parliament. It is important because the banks in my area specifically have shown leniency and the farmers have withdrawn from any aggressive action. But if we do not have measures that are identified and will address the problems, the whole situation may flare up, so much so that they will benefit neither the farmers, nor the banks, nor in the long run the government.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to follow the hon. member who has moved this motion. In moving the motion he has pointed out the seriousness of the situation, and in particular the very real difficulties which are being felt by farmers, small businessmen and Canadian industry as a result of the Canadian government's interest rate policy.
I must confess to a certain sense of frustration, having spent a great deal of time this session arguing that the government's policies do not make any sense and, that they are having a very harsh effect on Canadians. Also, convinced as I am, and as our party is, the harshness is essentially futile in that the government is lingering under certain illusions with respect to the consequences which this policy it is following will have on inflation.
We have heard from the minister, and we heard from him again in question period today, that this was the only policy the government can follow which will have an anti-inflationary effect. We have heard the same statements from the minister in different ways. I took some interest in reading the speech he made while he was in Paris attending the OECD meeting. The minister seemed to align himself with those, particularly in the United States and Britain, who have taken the view that the way to fight inflation, which is causing such problems not simply for the Canadian economy but for all western economies, is to carry on with the restrictive monetary policy, that this is the essential ingredient in the war on inflation.
I want to say to the minister that I do not think we can carry on very much longer with a sense of confidence that this policy is really having a great deal of effect. For example, he made much of the fact today that the demand for loans was still very high and was, in fact, inflationary.

Consumer loans.
June 26, 1981

Yes, he mentioned consumer loans. He went through a range of areas where the demand for loans was causing this kind of inflation. I have mentioned to him, and 1 mentioned it again today during question period, that the evidence from Statistics Canada released just this week is that demand for consumer loans, personal loans, dropped very substantially in the past year by 60 per cent. The demand for small business loans dropped 47 per cent in the first quarter of 1981. That tells us something. It is a signal that the government must look at the situation, that we do not have interest rates which in a sense reflect the demand pull. We have interest rates which reflect the policy of the government with respect to the Canadian dollar. That is the hard fact of the matter.
The root of the interest rate policy of this government has, for some years, been a conviction that protection of the value of the dollar at a certain level was the sine qua non of its anti-inflation policy and that interest rates had to respond to events in the United States in order to protect the value of the dollar. Even if one accepts the premise about the dollar- though this is not the terms of the discussion today and I do not want to go into it at length-the consequence for the domestic economy is something that has to give rise to concern. The minister's answer to that has been to say that growth in the Canadian economy has been fantastic. We had fantastic growth in the last quarter of 1980 and we are experiencing it again in 1981.
I say to the minister that I suppose it depends from what point you see the growth. If you look at the basic rate of capacity utilization right across the economy, I do not think there is any great cause for optimism. I do not think the economy is working at full capacity or that it is the nature of domestic activity in the economy which is really driving our rate of inflation up. I do not think there is any evidence to suggest that is the case.
I am reminded of the debate we had a couple of weeks ago in the House when the chairman of the Economic Council of Canada was before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs talking about productivity. The Minister has frequently talked about increased productivity as being the key to breaking this inflationary cycle in which we find ourselves. There is no question that increasing productivity of Canadian industry would do a great deal to reduce inflation. However, there was one thing which the chairman of the Economic Council of Canada made very clear, and he made it very clear in his report, and that is that, you cannot hope to increase productivity when the economy is being kept down at the level of capacity it is now.
This is the argument that should be going on in public with respect to the policies of the Bank of Canada. If we are serious about breaking the inflationary cycle, we are under a tremendous illusion if we think the way to do that in the current world context is to keep capacity down, working at far less than real potential. It will cause hardship in the economy.
Economic Policies
That is the inevitable, tremendously uneven effect of interest rates and inflation. This government is committed to an interest rate policy for reasons of exchange controls. The only kind of exchange control the government is prepared to contemplate is interest rate policy. That has been the case so far. Its interest policy is a form of exchange control. The government must face the task as to what other measures can be taken, fiscal, economic and planning, to deal with the consequences of high interest rates.
Let us look at the economy and the effects interest rates are having on patterns of home ownership and small businesses. There are problems of concentration in the economy. Real problems must be faced by the average businessman as a result of the fantastic cost of credit.
The farm industry was spoken of eloquently earlier. It is also affected. There is no sign of any letting up because the minister is convinced his policy is absolutely necessary. If we continue with this policy, it will have a devasting effect on the average Canadian businessman, home owner, potential home owner and farmer.
1 want to deal briefly with those three sectors. First, I want to reiterate the point I made earlier with respect to the farm industry. I honestly do not see how a policy which restricts supply can be described in a sensible way as anti-inflationary. The minister mentioned in particular the hog and cattle sector. Credit has become the largest cost to the farmer. The level of indebtedness of farmers is fantastically high. Farmers are being driven out of business.
We have had in this House personal, anecdotal and statistical evidence, evidence of all kinds. The minister says it is not relevant because the number of bankruptcies is not that high. Bankruptcy is the end of the road. A lot of things happen before somebody goes into bankruptcy. They cut down on supply, sell off parts of the operation, go into a joint venture with somebody else for part of the operation, attempt to refinance, or sell the farm to a larger corporate entity, such as is happening in many parts of Ontario and right across the country. These things happen well before a farmer goes into bankruptcy. That is why looking at the absolute number of bankruptcies as an indication of what is going on in the agricultural sector is not a realistic way of assessing the problem.
The statistics merely show that the problem is much more severe now than last year. We did not need statistical confirmation of something we already knew. The fact is that farmers are being driven off the land. We are encouraging the process of corporate concentration and agribusiness and destroying the family farm. That is what the government's policies are doing. That is the slow, steady, persistent impact of the government's policies right across the country with regard to agriculture.
We have a Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who sometimes thinks he is the minister of finance. The other week he was in the town of Nukko Lake in north central British Columbia to speak at a farmers' convention. At that time he produced the Nukko Lake manifesto, the personal manifesto of the Minister of Agriculture. The Canadian Press report of

June 20 reported the minister as saying that "some serious work is being done about changing the banking system in this country." He must be referring to the work of the NDP; I do not know what else he was talking about. He said the government will change the banking system if the chartered banks do not do something to help farmers.
The Nukko Lake manifesto was not the first manifesto of the Minister of Agriculture. We have had a number of them. They are amusing examples of an attempt to establish himself as a populist candidate in the one day, some day, forthcoming Liberal leadership race. It is a condemnation of our process when the Minister of Agriculture pretends that the government is serious about the effect interest rates are having on farmers. The minister pretends the government is doing something about the banking system and interest rates. The Nukko Lake manifesto, to put it bluntly, is an example of the big lie. Either the government is doing something about the banking system or it is not.
An aide to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the news report does not say who, stated "it is all new to me". In the House the next day the minister stated that he had no intention of reviewing the Bank Act. The government sent the Minister of Agriculture to deliver himself to various farmers groups. He was to tell them that the government was serious about doing something with respect to the banking system. However, we know it is not serious.
In conclusion, the government's policies do not make any sense to the average Canadian. It is becoming increasingly difficult for a home owner in a housing development who must renew his mortgage at 18, 18'A or 19 per cent while his next door neighbour with exactly the same accommodation is paying 12, 13 or 14 per cent because he bought at a different time. That is the roulette, arbitrary, random, and totally unfair effect that interest rates are having on Canadian consumers and businessmen. Eventually the government will have to recognize that it has a responsibility to minimize, even out and bring some rationality into an interest rate policy which affects people in ways that at the moment are totally arbitrary.
I see that the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) is shaking his head. When he gets up he will deliver himself of a Friedmanite defence of the government. We have the Fried-manites and Senator Lamontagne in the other place, and the minister somewhere in the middle telling us that he is not quite sure what the message is that he will take to the Summit; it will be on the one hand or the other hand. We have the Nukko Lake manifesto from the Minister of Agriculture.
We have the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) talking about the need for child tax credits. However, when it comes right down to it, the government is not doing anything with respect to the real effect that these policies are having on the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure today to speak to this opposition motion which condemns the government for failure to bring in effective economic policies to deal with what the hon. member has termed "the present economic crisis", and in addition to that to end the squeeze that disastrous interest rates are placing on small businesses and others in our economy.
The interesting thing about that motion is that it says there is an economic crisis and, in addition to that, a squeeze caused by high interest rates. If I could, I would like to try to deal with the question of the economic crisis first and then move on to discuss the interest rate situation. What are the underlying causes of the current interest rate situation? What are the alternative policies open to the government? I want to try to explain once again to hon. members opposite precisely why it is that the government is pursuing the policy it is.
To my mind, the motion is rather nonsensical because by any standard there is no economic crisis in this country today. There are high interest rates, to be sure. We all admit there are high interest rates, and we know the impact high interest rates have on a large number of people. However, to talk about an economic crisis is to talk about masses of people being out of work. It is to talk about economic growth which is in recession proportions or depression proportions. "Crisis" has a very real meaning to the public, and to us as well, and certainly "crisis" does not describe the situation facing our economy today.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I see the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is going right up his tree. That is not unusual.
Let us look at the economic indicators which are usually used to define "crisis" in an economic sense. Economic growth in the fourth quarter of 1980 was, at an annual rate, over 9 per cent. The long-term potential growth of the economy is generally accepted to be somewhere in the range of 3 per cent or 3.5 per cent, but we are talking about an annual rate of growth of over 9 per cent. That is phenomenal growth. What happened in the first quarter of 1981? Annual growth was over 4 per cent, still above the long-term average potential growth of the economy. There is no crisis in economic growth.
The unemployment rate now stands at 7.1 per cent, the lowest rate since 1976. Over 61 per cent of the Canadian
June 26, 1981

working age population is now working. That has been the case for the last two months, and that again is a historical record for Canada. In the last 12 months this economy has generated over 417,000 new jobs. There is certainly not a crisis in job creation. There is certainly not a crisis in unemployment. There is certainly not a crisis in economic growth.
The problem we face is the problem of inflation and the consequent high interest rates which follow from a high level of inflation. The policy of the government is designed to attack that inflationary problem and get it under control so that growth, employment, inflation and job creation will all be at levels we want to see.
The government brought forward its framework for economic policy in the budget on October 28. Hon. members have been saying that that economic policy was inappropriate in one way or another ever since the budget. The budget brought forward a balanced approach to economic policy. It did not go holus-bolus after the deficit in an attempt to reduce it at all costs. Nor did it go after inflation in that way. We did not say we would beat inflation regardless of the cost. The government took a balanced approach to try to ensure that minimal damage would be done to the economy, and in a great many areas, as indicated by the statistics I have just quoted, the government is succeeding quite well.
What was that policy? First, it was to hold the rate of expenditure growth within the trend growth of the gross national product over the next four years. We are working on that policy well. We are achieving those results.
The second aspect was to reduce the deficit and financial requirements over time. The figures given in the budget respecting deficit reduction and financial requirement reduction were in fact exceeded in 1980-81. Our deficit was $1.4 billion below what the budget forecast. Financial requirements were $1.8 billion below what the budget forecast. That part of the program is being attacked with success.
The third goal was to reorder priorities toward economic development, industrial adjustment and manpower retraining-in other words, to try to put in place those policies which would lead to a stimulation of economic growth and development in the country. We know there is work going on now on the final phases of an industrial strategy. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) has been working on that, discussing it in his speeches and so forth. The just announced textile policy will help that particular industry adjust to higher rates of competition and to the removal of trade barriers over the next five to six years. That is a policy of industrial adjustment which is extremely important, not just in this part of the country but across the country. There are textile workers in Vancouver and Winnipeg as well as in Quebec and Ontario. That is an extremely important policy.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) has announced a number of manpower training programs and employment-generation programs, and he will be announcing further programs.

Peanuts.
Economic Policies

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Regardless of the comments of hon. members opposite, these policies are working and they will continue to work.
The fourth part of the policy of the government as brought down in the budget was a monetary policy consistent with a reduction in inflation. The government is supporting the efforts of the Governor of the Bank of Canada to bring down the rate of growth of the money supply so it will be more in line with the real output of the economy.
That is a balanced economic policy which, as I said, has not only had, but will also continue to have, successes on a wide range of fronts. Not only is it a balanced policy, but it is also a consistent policy.
Consistently bad.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
We have been saying for some time now that what the business sector is demanding is consistency, stability of policy and a certainty that it knows what the government is going to do in the area of economic policy. That is precisely what this government is attempting to provide. The government is attempting to provide a balanced economic policy. It is not a stop-go policy, it is a balanced policy. It has been well announced, it has been followed, and we intend to continue to follow that policy in order to provide that kind of stability and confidence in the business sector.
We have heard much from the other side about disagreement among economists and other observers as to economic policy. I would like to tell hon. members that that simply is not true. There is not disagreement on the fundamentals of the policy. There may be disagreement with regard to the extent to which certain levers are pushed or pulled, but there is no disagreement on the fundamentals of the policy. All economists, economic observers and analysts are indicating-and they agree with us-that there is a need for both monetary and fiscal restraint if we are to beat inflation. There is no question in the minds of any of those observers that inflation is the number one problem which has to be beaten if we are to get the economy back on a long-term path of growth and prosperity. That is precisely what the policy of the government is intended to do. Its goal is to get the economy on a long-term growth path in order to provide prosperity and growing wealth for Canadians, stable price levels and lower interest rates by far than those we have now.
What about the opposition? From what we have heard for the last many months I would say that the opposition parties are totally confused as to what is appropriate economic policy and what is not. Now, Mr. Speaker, what do we hear? We hear cries from the opposition that we should immediately take steps to reduce interest rates. On the other hand, they say we must get the rate of inflation down.
Herb Gray said he would resign.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I intend to show very shortly that those two objectives are mutually inconsistent. If we are to bring interest

rates down immediately, the only result can be much higher inflation and consequently much higher interest rates in the very near future.
Another point, Mr. Speaker, is that we are being asked all the time-in fact, the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. j i Gurbin), who 1 respect as a conscientious and hard-working I member of this House, asked us again today-to expand expenditures; in this case, the small busines development bond, but in other cases it is mortgage interest and property tax credit, assistance for farmers, assistance for this or that group, assistance for consumer borrowers.
