speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Let us look, Mr. Speaker, at one of their options. Hon. members opposite say we should reduce interest rates immediately. Let me try to indicate what that would mean. It is clear our goal of reducing inflation over time will lead to lower interest rates; there is no doubt about that. If the policy is adhered to, as inflation comes down so will interest rates. However, I think the opposition misunderstand the causes of the current high interest rate situation. As a result they do not understand which remedies are possible and which are not.
As I have said a number of times, there are three factors contributing to the high interest rate situation. The first is the rate of inflation. If you annualize the monthly rate over the last four or five months, we have rates of inflation in the 13 per cent range, perhaps more. There is no way in the world people saving for retirement, to buy a house or for other reasons can be expected to lend their money for less than 13 per cent. If they do, the money they get back next year is going to be worth less than it is today. So the rate of inflation is always the bottom level for interest rates. You have to add to that the right savers have to at least some real rate of return, perhaps one or two percentage points above inflation. If you do that, you already have about 14 or 15 per cent. Then if it goes through a financial intermediary who is paying 15 per cent for savings, they have to have enough to at least cover their costs, so let us add another one and a half points. Now we have 16 or 16.5 per cent. Somewhere in there is the bottom line on interest rates today given the inflation factor. That is the primary driving force behind our high interest rates.
Now, on the other hand we have, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) indicated this morning, a fantastic demand for credit from a number of sources. When you couple that with the fact that now and over the last two to three years the Bank of Canada has been gradually reducing the growth rate in the money supply, you have a reduction in the credit available through the financial system at the same time as you have a big demand for credit because of inflationary expectations or other reasons. Those supply-demand considerations tend to push up the real rates of return individual savers demand.
The third factor, Mr. Speaker, is one which has been raised and bandied about on both sides of the House; that is, the high rates of interest available to Canadian savers in the United States. Those pressures are very real, but as the minister indicated this morning, we have not said and are not saying now that the U.S. interest rate situation is the only factor causing our high interest rates. The underlying cause is the inflation factor exacerbated by this demand-supply divergence.
I think to a great extent inflationary expectations are caused by the fact that a great many people say the government is not going to bring inflation under control; they are not really serious, they are not going to stick to the policy. As a result, they say they had better borrow and buy today because inflation is going to be a lot worse tomorrow.
Those inflationary expectations have to be broken, and the only way to do that is if the public becomes convinced the government is in fact going to stick to its policy. If the government reversed itself on this policy, you can count on inflation going right through the roof along with the expectations of inflation, with interest rates going even higher.
So, Mr. Speaker, we hear from the opposition members that the way to solve our high interest rate situation, to bring interest rates down, is either by decree or by putting on exchange controls; that if we do that and stop money flowing to the United States, interest rates will immediately tumble to 12 per cent. Well, Mr. Speaker, it just is not so. The basic
June 26, 1981

underlying inflationary situation in this country would not allow that to happen. The credit supply and demand in this country would not allow that to happen.
The situation we have now is that the market is far stronger than the Bank of Canada. There is no way the Bank of Canada can stand out in the street and by decree say interest rates will be such and such. The bank simply does not have that kind of leverage or muscle to go against the dictates of the market. The market is setting those rates, the treasury bill rates. Hon. members are saying yes, but the Bank of Canada is in there back and forth, in and out. But the effect of that is of the second order of small; it is minimal. The bank cannot stand against the wind week after week. If the tide is coming in, it is coming in; if it is going out, it is going out. The bank can moderate fluctuations but it cannot stand against the tide. That is the truth of the matter, Mr. Speaker.
It is not a policy of the government to say interest rates will be such and such. We have an inflationary situation in this country that we have to deal with. We have demand-supply conditions which are necessary if we are going to get inflation under control. And, of course, the last factor is the U.S. interest rate situation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to summarize, how do you reduce interest rates? You do it by bringing down the rate of inflation. That, as I said, cannot be done by decree. The bank could do two things perhaps to make a short-term dent in interest rates. It could give up control of the money supply. It could say we are going to flood the market with new money tomorrow.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that in the very short term that flood of new credit coming into the system would depress interest rates. But the effect over a period of six months to a year would be an acceleration in the rate of inflation and interest rates a year hence would be much higher. We have seen this happen in other countries where governments have decided the way to fight high interest rates was to flood the system with all the credit it can stand to put more pressure on interest rates in an attempt to bring them down; more money means that the price of money should be cheaper. The flaw in that logic is that more money in the system also creates excess demand, which creates inflation. Then we are faced with a situation where individual lenders say, "I will not lend at less than the rate of inflation or take a negative return on my savings". This means that interest rates go up as well. It is a fool's game. That option should not be followed.
I suppose hon. members of the NDP have put forward the other option, that the bank could simply say, "Let the dollar drop wherever it wants to go; by doing that, we will be completely independent of the United States, and its rates will not have any effect upon us". As I indicated earlier, there are two other factors which would tend to keep our interest rates up substantially within a very narrow band of where we are now.
Economic Policies
What would happen if we did that, if the dollar dropped substantially and interest rates came down? It would have an immediate inflationary impact. As soon as the dollar drops, everything we import from the United States or from any other country to which our currency is relatively depressed rises in price. Every product produced and sold in Canada, as well as being sold in export markets, rises in value in the export market. Therefore our producers are inclined either to send more of those goods into export, or they will raise the price here to match the price they can receive in export markets. Those two factors together mean an immediate burst of inflation in Canada and, once again, higher inflation leads to higher interest rates, not lower ones.
Another factor which should be considered is where it will stop. If we hold a differential between our rates and those of the United States, as was tried in Britain, the currency keeps flowing out. It is like turning on a tap. It does not only flow out for a short period of time, it keeps flowing out as long as the differential is maintained. Thus, how far down do we let the dollar go? Do we let it go down to 78, 75 or 72 cents? How far does it go down before interest rates are finally forced back up to stop it? It is a mug's game.
What effect will the decline in the value of the currency and its induced effect upon inflation have on wage settlements? Certainly when unions become involved in wage negotiations they ask, "What is the rate of inflation likely to be? We want at least to get that much as well as a real increase in our wages". If they see inflation accelerating the pressure will be to say, "No, we will not accept 12 per cent; we want 14, 15 or 16 per cent". But the pressure then builds upon wages. If such wage settlements are achieved we build in increased unit labour costs.
This is what happened in 1974. We were going through a period when suddenly there was an explosion of wage rates, with wage settlements at the 20 per cent range or more. This increased our unit labour costs and made them uncompetitive with those of the United States. Ultimately it led to a devaluation in currency to 83 cents, but it was largely responsible for the drop from $1 to 85 cents. There was a change in relative unit labour costs between the United States and Canada and the adjustment had to be made.
If we drop the value of our currency and it leads to inflation, which leads to higher wage rates here than in the United States or in other countries with which we trade, and our unit labour costs get out of line, it means the currency value will not recover. It is not a matter of dropping the currency value for a period of six months or a year, and then it will bounce back. It means we have ratcheted the currency down and it stays there.
The idea that we should go through a series of devaluations to solve our problem is a fool's game. It does not solve the problem. The problem is inflation; basically it is a monetary problem. It is one with which we have to come to grips and for which there is no easy solution. There is no painless solution to removing inflation from the system.

June 26, 1981
Economic Policies
We have heard comments about increased expenditures. To alleviate the difficulties caused by high interest rates, we are being encouraged to increase expenditures in a number of areas. Certainly they are laudable objectives, but where will those moneys come from? Should we cut defence spending? Some people would say yes. Should we cut economic policy spending to assist those who are being hit by high interest rates? Should we increase taxes or the deficit? Despite what members of the opposition say about their commitment to deficit reduction, if push came to shove they would say, "Let the deficit go up a little".
What does this mean? How much are we talking about? We hear that we are supposed to help home owners, farmers, fishermen, small business people and consumers. When we stop to think of it, we are talking about everybody. Everyone who borrows money is being adversely affected by high interest rates; there is no doubt about that.
What are we talking about in those four main areas-home owners, small business, farmers and others? I should like to deal with the small business development bond extension and the mortgage situation. The Conservative mortgage interest and property tax credit, if fully implemented, would have been a $3 billion per year program. The small business development bond program is already running in the $200 million range. If it was extended to finance inventories, which would mean that all small businesses could refinance their inventories under this program, we could be talking about half a billion, three quarters of a billion or a billion. The estimates are hard to come by, but certainly in those two areas we are talking about an increase in expenditures of between $3 billion and $4 billion per year. If we increased the deficit by that amount in that fashion, I guarantee we would have to tell the Bank of Canada to forget about controlling the money supply and to buy our bonds because they cannot be put on the market. If that is the case, it will be inflationary and will cause higher interest rates.
If we do not tell the Bank of Canada to monetize that debt and we go straight to the market to float another $4 billion worth of bonds, we will put upward pressure upon interest rates because we will be taking additional revenues or savings out of the system. Thus, in an attempt to protect people against high interest rates we create conditions which in fact lead to higher interest rates. Again I say it is a fool's game. Either we have to come to grips with the problem and deal with it or forget it.
There is no way societies can allow inflation and all of its debilitating societal effects to persist, to accelerate and to worsen. We must come to grips with the problem. I am convinced the government has come up with a program which will work. It is a program which will bring inflation under control. It will lead to greater economic growth in the future. It will lead to prosperity. It is a balanced program. It is not one which singles out any particular group in society to suffer as a result of the policy to bring down inflation. In a very real way, all of us will have to take some of that pressure, and in fact we are all taking some of it.
In conclusion I should like to say that the policy has a number of possible alternatives, all of which are worse. The good Senator Lamontagne from the other place indicated another possible alternative, effectively saying we could bring on some kind of an incomes policy and turn loose monetary policy. As I said before, that is like putting the kettle on the stove, sealing the top and turning up the heat. The only thing one gets out of that is an explosion. The only question is, when does one get it? Is it sooner or later? Therefore, that is a policy option which should certainly not be followed by this government, and I would certainly not recommend it.
With that in mind, I would like to conclude by saying that certainly and stability of policy are required in the system now. The public must be assured that the government is serious about the fight against inflation in order to beat inflationary expectations. Business must be assured that the government does not intend to follow a stop-go policy, if investment decisions are, in fact, going to reflect the long term policies of the government. In other words, what is needed in this country today is a balanced approach. That is what has been and what is the policy of this government.

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) gave us an elementary lecture in finance, but he did not tell us that a succession of Liberal governments got us into the mess in which we are today. Canada is today in a period of economic instability; there is no doubt about that at all. Its economic performance is much below its true potential and its capability. Repeatedly, Canadians today are worried about the changes to the Canada of the future brought about by the government's patriation package and its national energy policy, inflation and lack of or changing over-all industrial and social policy, and by increasing instability in the world at large.
I want to look backwards a bit, before I look forward, to see what has happened in Canada over the last three and one-half decades since the war, because it is a period in which successive Liberal governments have generally been in power. 1 want to list about eight areas of considerable importance in the growth of Canadian society, and then look at some of the problems that we have to solve as a Canadian society from here on in, in the eighties.
First of all, let me say that we have been very generous in allocating funding for education. We have educated ourselves, as a people, to one of the highest standards in the world. Our education has been broadly based, with a wide, non-constricting and non-dogmatic perspective. It was moderately permissive and generally directed toward material rather than spiritual ascension. It followed predominantly, though not totally, the American mould. However, we have built into our social and economic structure an enormous technological and productive potential which we are really not using to its full capacity at all.
June 26, 1981

Second, we apply technology extensively. I speak as a person coming from the technological field. However, most of it was imported from the United States of America, through the media of the multinational corporations, though we have excelled in a few areas, but not very many, like nuclear energy. One of the most remarkable things is that an engineer or a technologist in Canada could simply pick up a phone and call someone in the United States for advice, for a solution or a piece of equipment. No other country in the world has the access to the technological might of the United States that we have in Canada. I have some concern that recently we have been acting as a government in moving toward cutting off this lifeline of Canadian progress, or throttling it to some degree.
We have extensively used the multinational corporations and their access to American developed technology. These corporations became dominant in owning our resources and our industrial wealth. As a nation, we became an intermediate manufacturing and exporting nation with declining competitiveness in world markets. Indeed, our competitiveness today is cause for considerable concern.
Third, economically and on an over-all basis, we have had phenomenal growth of our national economy, primarily based on the harvesting and selling of our vast resources by the multinational corporations. The Canadian economy grew by approximately four times in constant dollars during the last three and one-half decades. Our population only grew by about 75 per cent. Therefore, we became rich as a nation, though other nations surpassed us extensively in terms of productivity. We built in Canada a physical plant system of unprecedented inefficiency, and only now are we realizing it as world energy costs are skyrocketing. Our own economy is agonizing with high inflation and low productivity.
Fourth, economically and socially the nation experienced an intense preoccupation with security against almost every eventuality: sickness, unemployment, old age, catastrophe, business bankruptcy, etc., mostly backed or sponsored by government action. We built a humane society based on government redistribution of wealth. Our system adopted tenure as a right rather than a privilege tempered with responsibility. We provided undisputed tenure to our civil servants, professors, teachers, professions, and thereby generated an increasing demand for tenure without productivity requirements in all of organized labour.
With increasing tenure, productivity waned. We became lazy, and the pride of doing was replaced with the enjoyment of loafing. Elaborate procedures and refined specialization became a substitute for performance. We demanded more and more from our governments, and governments acquiesced to the public demand.
Fifth, we became preoccupied with enjoying all the material goods of life at an increasingly younger and younger age. Homes and suites and cars and goods of all sorts were demanded and extensively promoted for the young. In providing all these goods, we established a vast credit system to give us what we wanted now, and increasingly mortgaged our future because we bought most of it on debt. Mass advertising
Economic Policies
created the appetite. Credit provided the means. Mass production and technology and imports provided the goods and lowered prices. We spoiled ourselves, and obsolescence, redundancy, style, throw-away and fraud prevailed. Our appetite increased and our frugalness decreased, and we damned the future and lived for the present. We continued to demand more and more from governments.
Sixth, yes, we demanded more and more from our governments, and our governments grew dramatically and involved themselves in every facet of our lives. Governments at the three levels grew without attention to political ideology or rationality or prudence. Politically, we dashed madly toward de facto socialism, with the three levels of government this year expected to tax some 43 per cent to 45 per cent of the gross national product of Canada and redistribute it. Governments have engaged themselves massively in wealth redistribution at rates which exceed the nation's ability for wealth production. Our appetite as government is so voracious that massive debt formation has overwhelmed us. I expect that the deficit of the federal government alone will be in the order of $15 billion this year. In the past, as debt rose we printed more money and in doing so institutionalized inflation rates in double digit figures. Of course, we have high inflation. As governments we have caused it with uncontrolled spending and lack of productivity over these last several decades, but particularly over the last four or five years.
What is inflation, Mr. Speaker? It is a reminder of the reality that we are living beyond our means; that we are getting poorer and must increase our productivity and competitiveness as a nation. Instead, we borrow more, print more money and delay the final reconciliation with fiscal prudence. But we all know that we cannot escape. Finally the government has found some backbone and now says we cannot escape; we have high inflation and we have to live with it. That realization is amazing after all these years. The unfortunate thing is that in the period of readjustment it is the poor and the needy, the weak and the old who suffer most. The time for readjustment is here. It is the poor and the needy, the weak and the old and the small businessman who are going to suffer most.
Politically our nation has evolved peacefully. Partisan politics has become ideologically blurred with all parties moving significantly for greater socialization and greater government involvement in the economy. Provincial governments have grown and gained significantly in posture and prominence over the national government in the last several years.
For a while, the world around us grew in stability but it is now beginning to come apart at the seams. Political, social and economic instability is increasing. World-wide inflation is causing a severe form of economic dislocation. Economic issues, resulting primarily from nationalistic protectiveness and resource pricing policies, are now foremost in the minds of world leaders. The risk is that the operation of the international economy may spin out of control and present a more grave

June 26, 1981
Economic Policies
threat to world order today than even the nuclear arms race or the struggle between differing political ideologies. The high rate of inflation is testing democracy itself as it has not been tested for the last several decades.
That, in a nutshell, Mr. Speaker, is the situation, both internally and externally, that is facing Canada in the eighties! Have we built a strong financial and economic house? I think we have built a house upon shifting sand. We have many adjustments to make and many difficult problems to overcome in the eighties. I should like to set forth some of them.
First, can we revise our economy and re-establish private enterprise as our motivating force for accelerated wealth production or, at the very least, can we find a workable and productive partnership between the private and public sectors? It is going to be difficult. The former Progressive Conservative government, which was in power for only nine months, attempted a beginning in this area.
Second, can we contain the voracious appetites of governments and restrain their growth rates by re-establishing the community, the home and the family unit as the prime motivator, caretaker and babysitter of the social dislocations of our society, instead of turning over those problems increasingly for governments to solve? We must make a start in this direction at the earliest opportunity.
Third, can we in the organized workplace rediscipline ourselves to increase productivity and innovation and the deployment of new technology to improve our competitiveness in the national and international marketplace? We have an example of this today in the Post Office dispute and the impending strike. This was our intent and policy as a Progressive Conservative government during the nine months we were in power. What initiatives has the present government evolved? What direction is evident in its policies for dealing with labour-management relations and the resulting low productivity?
Fourth, can we control inflation and its ravaging effects upon the less fortunate? To a large degree I accept that the present administration is a victim of American dictation and follows the U.S. interest rate structure like a child. It has literally no other option. It has not built in any options within the last decade, although it could have. There is no nation that has the potential for building economic options that we in Canada have with our vast resource potential and our resources going out of the country as raw material. The capacity to upgrade our own resources is immeasurable and would increase wealth in the country, but we need definitive and honest and difficult federal policies put in place.
Fifth, can we meet the challenge of energy self-sufficiency in all forms of energy use, and in particular, will we be able to meet the world food crisis resulting from environmental, climatic and population growth patterns? The next five to ten years will be critical in regard to world instability, and perhaps the North-South conference in two weeks' time is an omen of the critical conditions developing in the world.
Sixth, will we be able able to cope with the inherent economic and social restratification needed to cope with an increasingly aging population? We must examine seriously our pensions systems and anchor them to a more solid financial foundation than that which exists today.
Seventh, will we be reaching for greater brotherhood rather than increasing isolation in our urban conglomerates as we move toward a new century of civilization? Will equalization serve us well in the future so that Canadians everywhere in this vast country can enjoy a standard of living second to none in the world? Because we have the capacity.
Eighth, can we meet the challenge of constitutional patria-tion and redefinition and renewal to truly represent all regions in a national institution in the eighties? I think we can, Mr. Speaker.
In particular, we must permit those areas of our nation which have enormous capacity for growth, like the west, to grow without undue throttling. We must immediately undertake incentive policies to upgrade our resources before they I enter international trade. What is needed is boldness, courage, openness, analysis and action. The parliamentary secretary mentioned balanced economic policy and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) repeatedly referred to gradualism. If there ever was a time for boldness and courage and substance and analysis and action, it is now. Timidity, trying to help everyone at the same time, or gradualism is hardly a policy that will build a viable, progressive, dynamic economic and industrial sector in this nation in the next decade.
In conclusion, let me read the resolution we are discussing:
That this House condemns the Government for failing to bring before Parliament effective economic policies to deal with the present economic crisis and end the disastrous interest rate squeeze on the small business, industrial and agricultural sectors.
Of course we have a crisis in the nation. There are two kinds of crises. One might be likened to the idea of an egg falling off a ten-foot high fence and smashing to bits. The other crisis is a snowball rolling-

The second type of crisis is the one which can be likened to a snowball rolling downhill which gathers momentum and grows larger and larger with greater and greater force. I suggest that if we do not move fairly soon as governments in the nation in this area of strengthening the economy, we will have a second order crisis in our economy five or ten years from today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) in his closing remarks drew the attention of the House to the wording in a close reading of the motion before the House which gives me an opportunity to begin my contribution to the debate today. 1 draw the hon. member's recollection to this time last year when the first piece of legislation with which I had the honour to be associated in this House was an act to increase grants for assistance to municipalities. This legislation, hon. members will recall, increased the amount of money transferred by the federal government to municipalities in lieu of taxes.
It is an obligation of the federal government to pay for municipal services afforded to federal properties located in areas right across the country. It was a distinct pleasure, because of my past experience with municipalities, to be able to say that the federal government was providing $25 million extra which would be, I am sure, an advantage to those municipalities when it came time for them to look at the way they were carrying out their responsibilities and when it came time for them to strike their tax bills. In turn, that would have a direct impact on the ability of home owners, small businessmen and industrialists right across Canada to pay municipal taxes.
The hon. member has indicated he faults the government for taking action to assist in the economy of this country-I give that example to counter specifically those clauses of the resolution before the House this afternoon. It is not necessary, thank heaven, for the Government of Canada, in all of the things it does to address the economy, to come before the House with specific legislation, word, period, comma, semi-colon, in order to address the community at large. I say thank heaven for that. Quite frankly, as a new member of this House, again with my background in municipal politics, I was appalled that it took this House two months to debate an amendment to a constitutional resolution. This was an amendment put by the party opposite which now complains that this government has not brought legislation into this House for action to address the economy. How could we have done so when we were held up for a full two months on one resolution? You are aware, Mr. Speaker, of the acrimony that was introduced in this House. Yet, at the same time, the opposition complained about the government not taking action. The opposition can hardly complain that we are taking no action when in essence the opposition hijacked Parliament, which is a forum for addressing these problems.
What have you done since then?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) invites me to go to the next part of my speech. What have we done since then?
I was privileged to attend a meeting with the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) with representatives of the Trust Companies Association of Canada yesterday afternoon. We took that step to meet with representatives of the private sector who have a
Economic Policies
large segment of their portfolio directed toward assisting home owners. We met with these people because of statements made by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) who alleged there existed a crisis and widespread foreclosures and defaults in home ownership.
I shall cite some facts and figures which were obtained yesterday from representatives of the national trust companies holding the major portfolios for mortgages in Canada. In the case of the Royal Trust, foreclosures have reduced, not increased, from .34 per cent to .27 per cent in the year since the legislation to which I referred was introduced in this House. In that year it shows that the figures are for conventional and high ratio loans and the trend is actually downward, while there has been an increase in the amount of mortgages taken out during that period of time.
Canada Permanent Trust reports the same thing. In recent months, the situation of arrears of three months or more has actually improved. Montreal Trust reports the same thing. Montreal Trust indicates that, for example, in May, 1981, compared to May, 1980, the default rate was .35 per cent compared to .41 per cent. National Trust repeats the same experience with the figures given. Victoria and Grey reported a picture similar to the other companies. In May, 1981, the percentage of legal action commenced on borrowers was .07 per cent.
Those are the facts in the area of foreclosures and defaults, and the hardship being experienced by people. There are fewer people experiencing these difficulties, and those figures illustrate the situation up to the first of this month. Yet we still hear members opposite saying crisis. I do not know where they get figures to illustrate a desperate situation in the home owner renewal problem. I say that because facts show we do not need legislation. It has not been necessary in the year for the government to come with specific legislation in that area.
It was not necessary for we to receive instructions from the party opposite to meet, as I did, with the President of the Royal Bank of Canada on Tuesday morning of this week to get the same figures from him advising me that the crisis allegations of the members opposite are not founded on fact.
It was a concern for people over the differences in the interest rate this year as compared to last year, for those home owners and small businesses refinancing, and it was my concern for the difficult time these people are having that prompted me to raise this matter in Washington last week. I met with the secretary for housing for the United States, the HUD, housing and urban development, and the undersecretary for housing for the United States. I brought to their attention the difficulties being experienced by Canadians, especially those facing the roll-over problem, not to mention industry, as a result of interest rate increases.
As the member who spoke before me indicated, we have followed the world situation in terms of interest rates in order to have capital funds available to assist us in the housing industry and small business. If we did not do that, where

June 26, 1981
Economic Policies
would the capital come from? I addressed this issue of high interest rates with the secretary responsible for housing.
I had an opportunity to speak to senators and the House of Representatives leader in Congress. I indicated to them the adverse effect the high interest rate policy of the United States is having in this country. I gave the example of the government moving to do something in order to illustrate our concern. I pointed out the impact this is having on our domestic institutions such as banks and trust companies. I encouraged them to be sensitive toward Canadians who must renew their mortgages, as well as small business faced with the same situation.
What else has the government done? That is a gratuitous question because of no interruption. We have not had to come to the House, for example, to extend the AHOP plan, a provision which provides a safety catch or safety value for those facing an increase in interest rates in order to protect those people whose shelter costs exceed 30 per cent of their earnings. Those subsidy programs have been renewed.
Just two weeks ago the government announced, with regard to the assisted rental program, the subsidy would be increased on a per unit basis from $120 to $180 per month to attempt to address the hardship of renters.
What was the reaction of the housing critic for the official opposition? He maintained that increasing that subsidy was a benefit for the landlord. That is not true. We were concerned about 120,000 families which would otherwise face the inconvenience and hardship of disclocation as a result of foreclosure. We addressed the problem by introducing a subsidy which in the long run will result in a saving to the taxpayer.
What did we get from the opposition? We got criticism for taking the very steps that the motion before us today says we have not taken. The opposition has to make up its mind. For example, the MURB provision, reintroduced by the Minister of Finance in the budget last year had been allowed to lapse by the former administration. That administration was lauded by the previous speaker for its attention to those people in need.
The one provision of our tax system which has been identified as a useful and effective way of generating housing activity in this country is the capital cost allowance for construction of multiple buildings. It lapsed under the previous government and was reintroduced by this government in the budget. That move contributed considerably to a surge in the housing industry in the first quarter of this year. The annual rate of housing starts of 125,000 in June last year bounced dramatically to a rate of over 242,000 in the first quarter of this year, a five-year high.
The action of this government in supporting the industry with that capital infusion which encouraged developers was part and parcel of the resurgence of the industry. The hon. member says that the government is not concerned about the needy when it allows interest rates to rise dramatically. It was this government which moved to increase allocations under the National Housing Act for social housing starts of 25,000 to
30,000	last year in order to assist those in the modest income levels to have access to housing. The government has an
annual account of some $300 million which goes toward carrying the costs of some 400,000 existing social units. We felt it necessary to address the tight market situation in social housing, which we did, and we believe it has been a stimulant to the industry.
I will conclude with one final observation. I will contrast what this government has done with what was done in the nine-month regime of the last administration. The Matthews report recommended a withdrawal of support for all types of housing programs by the federal government. I have contrasted that with the initiatives we have taken. We have taken iniatives to work with the private sector to assist those facing hardship at this time. That is a stark contrast, one that I cannot help but make after hearing some of the comments made earlier in the debate today.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) has consistently, and one might say with fervour and almost with passion, supported the economic policies which this government has put in place. He justified them each time as he mentioned the cost to government of the various steps which have been taken. His most recent endeavour in this regard relates to the plea by members on this side of the House and by economists in Canada in general to extend the SBDL principle on a wider basis. He has justified the narrow and constrictive pattern in which this is exercised by saying "it will cost". That is purely and simply the Keynesian economic position, one that has been practised by this government for years. It is the negative approach to the cost of an incentive. It is not the positive approach of what the incentive would actually produce in other sectors of income for government. That is significant.
I think it must be recognized that as tax rates in the United States have gone down, revenues have gone up because of the stimulus to the economy. The member can treat this with scorn, as he has, but it would do him some good, his constituents some good and his small businessmen some good if he would just take a look at the other side of the coin, as some of us on this side of the House have tried consistently to do.
Government revenues do not go down in a stimulated economy, they go up. As the net gain of a stimulated economy under an extension of the SBDL principle to farmers, more small businessmen and more sectors of this economy will make the revenue of Canada not costly but incremental. I would imagine that little bit of an increase in mortgages just mentioned by the last speaker was probably more necessary to buy bread and butter than to buy new houses.
The agricultural aspect of this motion is intended to bring to the attention of the public the very critical position in which this industry now finds itself. It is no longer adequate for the minister to say repeatedly that we have the best farmers in the world and the best government in the world. The representations made to him, to the committee on agriculture and to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), coupled with the news of the performance of other governments around the world,
June 26, 1981

certainly negate the statement that we have the best government in the world as far as agriculture is concerned, and emphasizes the crass neglect by that government and that Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) who sits on your right, Mr. Speaker.
I certainly accept the statement that we have the best farmers in the world, but they probably receive the world's lowest recognition of their needs by means of this government's fiscal and monetary policy.
The European Economic Community, for instance, has established a fund which protects virtually every aspect of agricultural production of that area of the world against catastrophic losses which we are now experiencing. If there is no market at home, subsidies will be arranged for the disposition of surpluses somewhere in the world to the detriment of world markets and also to the detriment of those countries such as Canada which have been supplying the deficiencies of the world's food supply for years and are dependent upon its income. But no mercy is exhibited by that agricultural program.
In the United States there exists a multitude of laws of protection of agriculture against unnecessary hardship. We lack those laws. Imports can be controlled, bridge financing can be arranged and U.S. government purchases of surplus production has extended a stability to the economic structure of agriculture which we do not have the privilege of enjoying. Farmers today are borrowing money at a rate of simple interest as low as 12 per cent, and many of those farmers who are in beef feeding production are getting money for 16 per cent simple interest compared to the more than 20 per cent compounded on a monthly basis.
Former international trade negotiations have neglected to recognize the importance of this industry and its requirement for international markets. At the same time, to provide markets for other items for Canada in foreign markets, we have granted more favourable access to the Canadian market for agricultural products produced here. The combination of these two shortsighted policies has contributed in a major way to the economic difficulties we are presently experiencing.
Virtually every farm organization in Canada has made representations to this government pleading for reconsideration of both our international trade policies and our financial assistance programs which are so vitally needed at this moment in time.
Canadians as a whole recognize that certain industries need special considerations at special times and, as we in this House have done, have supported the policies of import quotas for the textile industry. Why then is it impossible for this government to recognize the need of such a vital industry as agriculture and to take prompt and immediate emergent steps to provide at least bridge financing for this industry?
Among the representations which have been made are those by the Canadian Horticultural Council pleading for recognition of the inflation factor as it applies to capital gains, and the recognition of the need of tax consideration for fuels and
Economic Policies
energy conservation materials used in the greenhouse industry. In these representations they have also asked for the small business loan limit to be increased to $200,000 and for the recognition of the accumulated requirement to consider the inflationary factor, along with an updating of the values established in the Advance Payments for Crops Act. These recommendations are made in what one may consider emergent economic circumstances and they need immediate and emergent response if these sectors of agriculture are to be helped. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture has made a representation to the Agriculture Committee, and I wish to read it into the record as follows:
Federal government failure to take immediate action to relieve the farm debt problem amounts to a scandalous lack of concern for the disruption of the lives and livelihood of growing numbers of family farmers.
An emergency farm credit program, through the federal farm Credit Corporation, is required to provide special refinancing for those farmers who are going under through no fault of their own.
Farmers hit hardest are hog and beef producers who are being destroyed by a combination of rising costs, low farm prices and stratospheric interest rates. Cash crop producers financing major inputs are also facing serious credit problems.
This is an emergency. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is most concerned about the increasing number of actual farm bankruptcies and foreclosures. The evidence is that there is a rising flood of farmers in trouble, and current bank interest rates are the crushing blow that will put them under. If this is not so, a federal emergency program will get at the truth and no harm done.
Farmers in this position who now have nowhere to go for help must have some program which will give them a chance for survival. Failure by the federal government to act and act quickly on this matter would be quite simply, irresponsible.
The federal government has the capability of launching an emergency program nearly overnight, at very little cost to the taxpayer.
Please note I am not suggesting the expenditure of money, but rather bridge financing. The brief continues:
1.	It has a fully developed, trained administration in the Farm Credit Corporation for doing the job.
2.	It has the capability of providing funds at more moderate and/or deferred interest rates in cases of special need.
3.	Surely it can get the co-operation of the banks not to foreclose on loans until the Farm Credit Corporation has a chance to review each applicant farmer's position and take necessary action.
The action being requested by the CFA does not require large government expenditures and subsidy. Funds provided to the FCC for lending are not a government expenditure. They are an investment and a good one, that will be repaid. Government budgetary practice that calls them an expenditure is a misnomer, and it is important not to be misled by it.
The CFA is requesting a helping hand to farmers with fundamentally sound farm enterprises who are being ruined while the FCC sits by unable to do the lending job which it can do and was created to do, because of lack of funds to lend.
It is not valid to argue that the increasing bankruptcies are a result of bad management on the part of people who don't deserve help. Let's have a program that can help those that should be helped. There will be a lot of them. We challenge anyone to say it was bad management because a farmer in 1978 or 79 didn't foresee interest rates at 20%, when the banks willingly lent them the money that has now become such a disastrous burden.
If the federal government does not act and act quickly on this matter it will be a black mark on its record. The CFA asks for assurance at once that the Cabinet is urgently considering this request. We believe a serious and responsible review of the matter cannot result in any other decision than to accept the action which we are proposing.

June 26, 1981
Economic Policies
Let me quote from the Toronto Star of May 18. The article is so pertinent it merits reading in full, but time will not permit. It states in part:
Canada's farmers are among those who are the hardest hit victims by the Bank of Canada's deliberate policy of high interest rates to battle inflation and when farmers for whom interest rates spell disaster in today's capital intensive agriculture are pushed into bankruptcy and farm abandonment, the entire economy suffers.
That is from the Toronto Star. Let me quote again from the same article:
Hugh Moss, a cattle farmer, says, "The only way I can afford to pay 20 per cent interest is if I get over $1 per pound for beef'. Right now he only gets 80 cents a pound and plans to sell off part of his farm to get the money to pay his debt... Ralph Barry, of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, estimates for every farmer who declares bankruptcy there are at least ten others who decide to sell their land and equipment and drop out of agriculture while they still have some measure of solvency. He says that this province loses about 1,000 farmers a year. It's got to stop.
Again from the Star, and I quote:
If Canada allows her agricultural community to be crippled by unmanageably high interest rates not only will we not be in a position to offset world shortages of food in years to come, we will also be at the mercy of the high cost of imported groceries.
Perhaps the most pertinent part of this article is the following:
Canada has traditionally recognized the particular and irreplaceable contributions that farmers and farming make to the economy by offering agricultural enterprise relatively low interest loans through the Farm Credit Corporation.
Please note that this did not come fron any farm magazine or farm organization. This is recognition by a non-farm paper of a crisis situation which exists. Let me quote again the traditional aspect of the last excerpt of this paper. It reads:
Not only has the traditional supply of money not been available through FCC, but traditional recognition of agricultural needs through price stabilization payments has been equally abandoned.
Two traditions are gone.
Antiquated cost of production figures, for instance, in the potato industry would indicate that if a price stabilization payment were to be made-
For this commodity.
-it would be made on the basis of something less than 60 per cent of the cost of production of this commodity.
Historically and traditionally the formula would have been on a stop-loss basis, not on a 60 per cent of cost basis.
Let me quote from The Financial Post of May 2 in respect of fruit and vegetable production in Canada as follows:
Fruit and vegetable cash receipts amounted to $770 million last year, with 31 per cent from fruits, 26 per cent from potatoes and 43 per cent from other vegetables. This is an industry with a big and growing trade deficit, more than one billion dollars last year.
I have gone out of my way to quote non-agricultural sources to substantiate the case for agriculture, and I believe that these quotes do that adequately. When The Financial Post says that we have a $1 billion trade deficit in the fruit and vegetable industry-and we can produce most of those fruits and vegetables-there is something wrong with the fiscal, monetary
and agricultural policy of this nation. 1 repeat that I have gone out of my way not to quote farm papers for this purpose.
On May 19 the Minister of Agriculture was interviewed on CBC. His principal theme was that the banks should do more. Apparently the banks have lent approximately $16 billion or maybe $18 billion to farmers, but the Government of Canada is not prepared to put even a part of a billion dollars at the disposal of the Farm Credit Corporation as an advance for bridge financing for agriculture.
The minister gave some economic history of his own and discussed the possibility of his making representations to the government for a better deal for agriculture, but as usual he could not be pinned down in this interview to an adamant statement of his own that he would in fact make demands of the government as the Minister of Agriculture. He just gave his usual evasive gobbledygook support to the government and was unwilling to take a positive stand on behalf of the industry he represents.
The time for ministerial reflections upon the great history of agriculture is now past. The time to consider what steps the government can and must take to extend financial assistance to this industry is now. Is it not as important as Chrysler and Ford? This does not imply criticism of aid to those companies. I merely wish to emphasize the neglect on the part of the Minister of Agriculture of the industry he so halfheartedly represents.
Representations have been made by every agricultural organization in Atlantic Canada pleading for a recognition of their plight. If the Minister of Finance and this government in general do not recognize disaster when they see it eyeball to eyeball, and if the Minister of Agriculture is not prepared to put his portfolio on the line, not only will the 76 per cent increase in farm bankruptcies grow larger but the total economy of Canada will also suffer.
If the government is not interested in farmers, it should be interested in the total economy of Canada and the impact on that economy of a declining agricultural industry.
Recently there has been criticism of the repetitive nature of speeches in the House of Commons. The previous speaker made a criticism regarding the time consumed in debate in this House. When we have a responsive government which recognizes ability across the floor as well as in its own hallowed and divine precincts and when there is compromise and joint planning, debates will not linger, they will not be extended, and we will be able to get on with the business of the House. But this House will not lie down in front of the introduction of regulatory legislation rather than legislative legislation. It will not lie down in front of the extension to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) or the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and extend to them the power to control by regulation the Minister of Agriculture and the policies which he should and must introduce. The Minister of Agriculture must have freedom to function in an independent and recommending way for his industry.

I received today a letter in response to some questions I asked in the committee on April 2. It took the minister two months and three or four weeks to respond. I asked for reconsideration of the feed freight subsidy in Atlantic Canada. That has been put over for study by the Feed Board of Canada in the face of absolutely pertinent and proven documentation making a case for an increment to the feed freight subsidy presented by a host of organizations from Atlantic Canada and eastern Quebec. It is going to be studied.
Potato production in Atlantic Canada is in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. A storage program for potatoes will take place in Kentville, Nova Scotia. With all due respect to Nova Scotia,, which has a small potato industry, the climate is not quite the same. Results from that station will be good, but this work should be done in the potato-growing area. It should be done either at Charlottetown or Fredericton, but not Kentville.
There is a Meristem program for agriculture and the promotion of better seed potatoes in Canada. There will be a conference on that in Ste-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere. The Meristem program is supposed to promote a better seed industry in Canada, but the seed industry is not in Ste-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere. The export seed industry for which this is designed-as well as for improvement in quality-is in Atlantic Canada, but the conference will be in Ste-Anne-de-la-Pocatiere. If the west does not just raise hell, no doubt we will soon be looking after rapeseed in St. John's, Newfoundland. That would be as logical as the answers I received.
Let me go one step further. The minister closes his letter by saying, "The program is in place". Fie was referring to several, one of which is the storage subsidy program for perishable products. Yes, the program is in place, but it is just like the subsidy program for the fishing industry. No money was put into it. The minister exhorts farmers to use a program for which he does not see fit to get any money.

The result is that the markets for these basic products of Canada except oil have declined in virtually every viable market except the United States. They have declined 24 per cent with respect to Britain because the pound is worth so much more; 21 per cent with respect to Germany; 10 per cent for Japan and some 21 per cent for Sweden.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Lapointe (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for recognizing me in this debate. Once again our friends opposite are talking about the disastrous interest rate squeeze on the small business and industrial sectors. The hon. member who had the floor just before me spoke of economic incentives and urged the government to go ahead with policies of exaggerated expenditures at a time when inflation is the most difficult problem to cope with. However, speaking more specifically of economic incentives to which the hon. member referred, in all likelihood he does not have time to read the newspapers or else he does not understand what he reads, Mr. Speaker. I read in the Financial Times of June 22, 1981 an article entitled "Government Aid to Business Now Tops $6 Billion a Year".
In that article the Financial Times lists a series of programs in the fields of financing, loan guarantees, labour training assistance, investment tax credits, research and development

June 26, 1981
Economic Policies
tax credits, as well as all the special programs we have implemented since we returned to office, Mr. Speaker, precisely to spur the economy and the industry.
Hon. Members of the opposition have such a limited understanding of the economy that every day they ask us: Where is your industrial strategy? Where is your economic development strategy? We would have to label each decision we take and say: You on the other side, wake up, because that is part of the industrial strategy. They keep forgetting certain achievements such as for instance the fact that as recently as last week we announced a strategy for the textile and clothing sector under which $250 million will be earmarked for the restructuration of businesses and for assistance to employees who might have to relocate as a result of our import policies. They also fail to mention that we have launched our $350 million industrial restructuring program which the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) had announced in his budget last October. They fail to mention our assistance program for the micro-electronic industry, another $50 million. As recently as this morning 1 was in Sherbrooke to announce that the local university would become one of the six leading electronic technology centres in Canada. A similar announcement was made in Vancouver, Edmonton, Winnipeg, Toronto and, as I just said, Sherbrooke, and within a few weeks we will be announcing another leading electronic centre in the Maritime provinces.
And then we have a bigger budget to promote productivity in defence materials. We also have the new policy in the field of exports where my colleague the Minister of State for Commerce (Mr. Lumley) has drastically increased the budget to boost export products and set up the mixed credits program. All this is part of an industrial strategy of major government investments. The Financial Times quotes a figure of $6 billion. 1 will not quote the government press release because my colleagues opposite will say that I am trying to mislead them, that is why I refer to a serious paper like the Financial Times, and I would suggest that hon. members read a little more economic publications in order to understand what goes on in that area.
Of course, some have again argued that high interest rates are the only cause of bankruptcies in the small business sector, and I would refer them once again to the Financial Times, because members across do not readily accept what we say. So I would refer them to an article published in the Financial Times of June 22, 1981, and I quote, Mr. Speaker: "Don't blame high rates for bankruptcies".

Dun & Bradstreet Canada Limited statistics of May 29, 1981, indicate that business failures are up 17 percent over 1980. We all agree with this figure, Mr. Speaker, but in the same publication Dun & Bradstreet reveals there is no concrete information to indicate specifically that high interest costs are causing small business to fail. The same study adds
that 97.6 per cent of the 1980 business failures were due to bad management.

So enough of this witch-hunt, of trying to prove that high interest rates are the cause of ever-increasing small business bankruptcies. These bankruptcies are tragic, of course, and it is harmful to the economy as a whole when companies are forced out of business, however we tend to forget that even though the bankruptcy rate was 17 per cent in 1980, the rate of increase or of creation of new small businesses was 20 per cent, Mr. Speaker. So we should take a closer look at what higher interest rates mean for small business.
Let us suppose, Mr. Speaker, that you are a small businessman and that your working capital or your line of credit at the bank is $100,000, and you know as well as I do that over 80 per cent of small businesses in Canada have working capitals and lines of credit under that amount. But let us take 100,000, it is an easy figure to work with, and let us say that last year or two years ago your working capital was costing you 12 per cent, now in 1981 it is costing you 22 per cent. Over a period of one year, that represents an additional charge of $10,000, but one has to consider the entire financial picture of a company before saying that interest rates are the one and only cause of bankruptcy. One has to remember that there have also been increases in the cost of electricity, oil, gas, telephone and rent, as well as in municipal and provincial taxes. So if one reviews these financial statements, Mr. Speaker, one realizes that the issue of increased interest rates is a relative one. There are several alternatives to deal with this additional charge of $10,000: cut the personal expenses of the owner, cut back on the inventory, review the hiring policy, and there are countless other ways that can be used in a fiscal year to allow a business to cut its costs by $10,000 in order to meet this increased charge.
We are being told that the government does not want to stimulate the economy. It is obvious, when we look at the figures, that the argument about the $6 billion per year injected in the Canadian economy is not valid. When they say that interest rates are the only reason why small businesses go bankrupt, I say that those people know nothing about small businesses or the balance sheet of a Canadian business. And when they say that the government has no strategy, no master plan, I say that those people are blind. As I said earlier, we will have to stick a label or ring a bell each time we take a decision and tell them "Wake up, this is part of the economic strategy of the government, we are putting forward programs to assist the Canadian economy".
I have commented some of them, but there are many others. A few weeks ago, my colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais), announced the Suppliers' Development Fund. With him, I helped organize throughout Canada the
June 26, 1981

exhibitions called Contact 81 through which we tried to put the government's major customers in contact with the smallest suppliers in each region, whether Vancouver, Calgary, Winnipeg, Toronto, Halifax or Montreal, so that major Canadian companies can find an increasing number of sub-contractors among Canadian suppliers.
During these nation-wide exhibitions, Mr. Speaker, we were able to identify 2,500 additional sub-contractors who will be able to market new products which we now have to import and some of whom will be able to benefit from the Suppliers' Development Fund to develop in Canada new products to replace imports. But my colleague, the Minister of Supply and Services, went even further. Ten months ago, last August, Mr, Speaker, I had the honour to announce in co-operation with his department our sub-contract program. Under this program, we decided as a government to use our purchasing power to improve the small business sector, make it even more active and give it more opportunities.
Under this purchasing policy, we indicated in 1980 that 39 per cent of all purchases would be from small businesses, which represents about $900 million. With the approval of the government, my colleague and myself decided that our target would be 45 per cent of all government purchases, and we want to spend through our purchasing policy $1.4 billion a year, which will be directly injected into the Canadian economy to help small businesses.
We are told that we have done nothing concerning interest rates. I would like to speak about another program which has had even more success than expected, namely the small business development bond program. My colleague, the Minister of Finance, announced this program in his budget, and my colleague, the Minister of State (Finance) (Mr. Bussieres), accepted my amendment to provide an extension of these bonds.
We now expect that, thanks to this government policy and under this program, banks and financial institutions in Canada will provide loans to small businesses wanting to purchase new equipment, expand their business, purchase land or expand their premices at a rate of about 10 or 11 per cent, or 50 per cent of the current business rate, and in this way inject $2 billion in the economy. I am not making up this figure. It was the figure quoted by the President of the Canadian Banking Association, a figure which we get when we add all the amounts that chartered banks and financial institutions allocate to the small business development bond. Two billion dollars, Mr. Speaker! The members opposite might think this is insignificant!
For my part, I believe that it is an absolutely fantastic amount which will enable the small business sector in Canada to continue to grow, to create employment, to develop new technologies and to make the Canadian economy healthy, because as everyone knows, and the government best of all, the small business sector is the most dynamic in Canada and was
Economic Policies
responsible for 62 per cent of all new employment created in Canada in 1980 and is responsible annually for 40 per cent of all employment.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we want to help this sector and this is why we have decided first of all to implement all these programs, such as the Suppliers' Development Fund and the Microelectronics Assistance Program, through which small businesses can obtain 100 per cent financing from the government for feasibility studies to determine whether electronics can be used in their business and can obtain subsidies of 75 per cent for the installation of electronic material and manpower training.
In addition to those programs and the obligation we have to promote the expansion of small businesses, the goal of our whole purchasing policy is to pour into the economy huge amounts of money to help, protect and develop this sector in which we believe.
Mr. Speaker, several indicators would lead us to believe that the policies we have initiated are working and helping small businesses. Before rising in the House, I was looking over that part of my annual report dealing with the Small Businesses Loans Act. In 1980, $400 million in loans were granted to small Canadian businesses involved in various activities, which is an increase of 72 per cent over 1979. And when we consider the figures for the first quarter of 1981, we realize that they represent an increase in value of 58.6 per cent over the corresponding period in 1980.
As far as the Federal Business Development Bank is concerned, over 40,000 small businesses in Canada are being assisted under various loans programs. In fact, over 40,000 businesses in this country are taking part in the Federal Business Development Bank's Counselling Assistance to Small Enterprises program; I could mention also the 50 per cent investment tax credit which was announced in his budget speech by my colleague the Minister of Finance, jointly with his colleague the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane) for the benefit of the less-developed areas of our country. This 50 per cent provision means that if you decide overnight to go to the Gaspe area, the Maritimes, northern Quebec or northern Ontario and to invest $100,000 to set up a small business and create jobs, you will get $50,000 back from the government. That is the way to stimulate the economy and develop this very important sector.
The opposition is complaining that interest rates are suffocating small businesses. It is a fact that we are going through difficult times, Mr. Speaker, but we have put in action the necessary mechanisms to alleviate this problem and help this section develop. Everyone knows as well as I do that today is an opposition day-

What opposition?

Economic Policies

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
-the Tory opposition who introduced a motion, according to them, of basic importance to the very future of this country. Too bad, Mr. Speaker, the television cameras cannot focus on their benches. Only one of my colleagues and friends is sitting there to represent my Progressive Conservative friends, Mr. Speaker. That just shows how interested they are in the Canadian economy. I approve the decisions and the directions taken in matters economic by the Minister of Finance when he tells us: I do not want to stifle the Canadian economy by making cutbacks that would hinder economic expansion. But, on the other hand, in view of the current inflation, I simply must cut spending to some extent. To my mind, the Minister of Finance advocates and follows, as well as the government, a policy of common sense through this inflation period. Let us not delude ourselves, Mr. Speaker, current interest rates are not a threat to our economic health, but inflation is. We must apply all our wits, all our tools and resources, all our economic levers to fight against the curse that afflicts not only the farmers, homeowners, individuals, small and big businesses, but absolutely everyone.
It is essential, in implementing the policy put forward by the Minister of Finance, that we pursue it in order to succeed in reducing interest rates and thus allow all sectors of our Canadian economy to thrive and all Canadians to enjoy an improved social and economic life. In my view, the motion put forward by the members of the Progressive Conservative party is practically meaningless and of no interest to those members, judging from the empty seats. And that motion disregards the facts as well as the major economic efforts of this government and our sensible policy.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity to address this House on the important motion placed before it with respect to the condemnation which we should have of the government for its inability to deal with the economic policies described in the motion and, in particular, with its inability to deal with the high usurious interest rates prevailing in Canada today. We very clearly recognize, and even hon. members from the government side, do so that those rate are excessive in terms of what they ought to in Canada. They have been officially established by the Bank of Canada, encouraged, promoted and prompted by direct government intervention and action. We can recall the days when we did not have the fixing of these rates by a Thursday auction of government bills, and when the government itself took the responsibility. Now the government does it in an indirect manner by instructing the Governor of the Bank of Canada as to what he should do. On Thursday of every week, we wait with bated breath to determine the interest rate which Canadian home owners will ultimately be paying, Canadian businesses will be paying, and Canadian consumers will be paying for the money that they borrow. Today, we have
an effective rate, as established by the Bank of Canada, at 19.08 per cent. That rate translates into an effective rate of between 22 per cent and 23 per cent for consumers who are fortunate enough to borrow their funds from conventional sources, and a similar rate for small businesses in Canada, and an effective rate of between 18 per cent and 19 per cent for those who are renewing mortgages or acquiring new mortgages for their homes.
The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) has commenced upon the fact that insolvencies and bankruptcies which have occurred in the small business community have, in large measure, been due to a number of causes and ought not to be directly attributable to the high cost of money. His suggestions are very interesting. He suggests that if one is, indeed, in the position of a small businessman who finds that on a $100,000 loan, to which he makes reference, interest has increased over $10,000 in a period of a year, what one should do is to cut down one's staff. He suggests that we lay off some people. A moment later he gets into an explanation as to how, if one wants to establish a small business in Quebec, or Gaspe or northern Ontario-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: I did not say that at all.

-that one can get a government loan to hire more people. I wish he would make up his mind. Does he want small businessmen to lay off employees, or does he want them to hire more? The fact of the matter is that in our country we rely, in large measure, for employment to be provided by the small business community in Canada.

speechtext: The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism on a point of order.
