speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 am sorry to interrupt the hon. member. I am not in the habit of doing so. Admittedly he listened patiently to my comments, but I would like to respectfully ask him not to try and mislead the House. At no time did I suggest that small businesses are laying off employees.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for York North has the floor.

It is regrettable that the minister cannot weigh his words appropriately so that they come out the same, both when he is talking about the cutting of employment and when he is talking about increasing employment. That is a common failing of the members of the government. I can well understand how he is led into that trap.
The simple fact of the matter is that this nation cannot survive on interest rates which are consistently and permanently in excess of 20 per cent. Rates of that nature will have the
June 26, 1981

direct effect of sucking the lifeblood out of the entire economy. It is the responsibility of the government to do something about it. Today in the House, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), in answer to one of my questions, relied upon the fact that the major enemy of government is inflation and inflationary expectations. I know the government relies on that fact. The minister said, upon return from a meeting of the OECD in Paris, France, that the object of the government is to break inflationary expectations. Those comments with respect to inflation and the need to combat it have been referred to by the hon. Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans).
However, the question is, has the government in fact taken the necessary steps to achieve its laudatory goal? The answer to that question is that very clearly it has not. This morning in the House I asked the Minister of Finance how he equated that objective with a bill which was passed by this House on Monday, Bill C-57, dealing with an amendment to the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act which included a provision therein for the fixing of tax on an ad valorem basis. I pointed out that in fixing that tax in that fashion, it was obvious to anyone who is aware of that bill and the changes to be brought about as a result of its passage, that the government, ever mindful of its need to grab more and more taxes from Canadians, expected that the price of the commodities subject to that tax would increase. The government, by its own legislation, has told the public in Canada that it expects the price of certain commodities to go up. How does it therefore equate its objective to break inflationary expectations when its own actions have indicated to the public that it believes that price in Canada will increase? Accordingly, it has encouraged the public to believe the very thing that it suggests it wants them not to believe. Not only has the government done that, but it has also taken more funds from the public and will continue to do so under this piece of legislation. Therefore, it has fuelled inflation itself.
Doubtless people are motivated by a desire to place in their own pockets, for their own purposes, and in the pockets of their families for their families' purposes, additional revenue. For that reason, Canadians have generally adhered to a work ethic in Canada. They believe that if one works harder and works longer, one will make more and keep more. In the event that the government tells them that it will cost them more to live because the government is taking more of what they earn, they will, indeed, want to earn more. That is a logical conclusion which the government, had it any wit at all, would recognize.
The more the government takes, the more the public will demand for both the services and goods produced by the public. That is fuelling the inflationary expectations and fuelling inflation itself. Yet the government sits back, and the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism suggests that it is appropriate to reduce one's staff or, indeed, maybe move one's plant to some other area in the country. The fact of the matter is that the public in Canada, small businessmen,
Economic Policies
farmers and fishermen, know best what to do with their funds. It is no answer for the government to invoke program after program directing the economy in a particular course. Businessmen in Canada know best what to do with their revenues. Businessmen will be better served if the government reduces taxes and establishes an economic climate in which they can flourish. Home owners are better served if their after tax revenues are higher so that they can look after their own needs. The public in Canada is not asking for a handout. They are asking for a hand off. And the hand off which they seek is the heavy hand of the Government of Canada.
These are the primary issues with which we should be concerned. Now I know that the Minister of Finance has indicated in this House that our real growth, after allowing for inflation, may well, on an annual basis, be in the neighbourhood of 4 per cent this year. He examines that annual growth and says that we do not have an economic crisis in this country. We can see that our unemployment rate is at a level which is lower than that to which we have become accustomed and that is recognized. Let us not dispute it. But that is today, Mr. Speaker. The wisdom of a government should surely be reflected in its determination to take steps which will affect the future of this country. I am not talking about the future in ten or 15 years, I am talking about the future around the corner, within six months when most people who have acquired homes at 18 per cent and 19 per cent interest, when those small businessmen who have expanded an operation and had to borrow money at 22 per cent or 23 per cent, recognize that after six months they cannot bear the interest charges. That is what is happening in this country. If the government does not realize it, I say it is shortsighted and should, in the words of this motion, be condemned.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Hear, hear!

We have heard the statistics. The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) read off some statistics which had been provided to him by various lending institutions. Those statistics referred to foreclosures on personal residences. The Minister of Public Works, before he came to this House, practised law. If he were to consult with people who are his former partners, he might well ask them to give him the figures for judicial sales of property or writs of possession. If he would add them all up, he would find the real measure of hardship among Canadian home owners because there has been a recent development furthered by the actions of the lending institutions, not to foreclose but, rather, to have judicial sales of property, even have writs possessions so that the homes may be extracted from the owner and rented, until a more appropriate time for a subsequent judicial sale may occur.
Those figures in themselves are meaningless, Mr. Speaker. He might also like to confer with his colleague in the House who is complaining about the fact that there were not very many Conservatives in the House when he was speaking and who has now left. He suggested that the small business com-

June 26, 1981
Economic Policies
munity was not in as bad a position as it might be, and in fact some of their financial ills might have resulted from an increase in hydro charges and real property taxes or business taxes on their establishments. The fact of the matter is he might well consult with him and determine what number of those small businesses have not been put into bankruptcy, and of course there are a large number who have, but who have been forced into voluntary liquidation. Some small businesses recognize that it is better to sell out now at whatever price than to lose everything by holding on another few months. In other words, these are the very people who foresee the path set for them by present government policies. But there is nothing said of that and there is relatively little concern shown for them.
Government action today, Mr. Speaker, is destroying the foundation upon which this nation has been built. It has been built upon the concept of hard work and prudence which would result, after a reasonable length of time, in individuals acquiring their own homes. It has been built upon time, hard work and the enterprise of individuals who wish to transform small businesses into large businesses in Canada, thereby not only offering the employment that the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism would like them to reduce, but at the same time building the nation. Policies which have been advocated by this government, that is to say, policies of shifting tax money, allocating funds to projects which the government thinks are important, have no regard for what the public thinks is important and what small businessmen and home owners think is important. Those are the issues which have prompted them to work and strive to achieve their goals.
This government has been the most know-nothing, say-nothing and do-nothing government this country has witnessed in a long time. Since it has taken office, inflation has spread and increased despite the fact that it has itself recognized that inflation is the chief enemy.
The government looks with some pride at the fact that perhaps the GNP may be increasing somewhat this year. But it does not pay heed to the hardship and the heartbreak that a lot of people must suffer. What action has the government taken since October 28 to curb the insatiable appetite for funding which it extracts from the public? It is true that inflation is indeed the core source for high interest rates in this country. But who is responsible for inflation? Is it the man who is working on the production line at General Motors? Is it the farmer who is selling his products and is obliged to sell at whatever he can obtain? Is it the fishermen, or the small businessmen?
The prime source of inflation, Mr. Speaker, is the government itself, and there are two ways in which this regrettable circumstance occurs. It is either as a result of the increase in the money supply or the extraction of more and more funds from individuals and businessmen in Canada, or both. In the first case, while this government and its predecessor Liberal administration were in office, we had circumstances where the increase in the money supply on an annual basis exceeded 14 per cent per year.
How can increases of that nature ever retard inflationary growth? The answer is that it cannot. Today, I give the government credit to some extent for the fact that through the Bank of Canada, it has reduced the increase in the money supply to something in the neighbourhood of 6 per cent. Mind you, that is still above even the projected growth in the GNP, but it is a marked improvement over the historical use of money supply by this government in the past to feed inflation in this country.
What about the second element of the true growth of inflation? I do not have the statistics for today, but the last ones I saw showed the federal government extracted 43 per cent of the total GNP. In the United States, the federal government there extracted 31 per cent over the same period of time.
I know the response of the Minister of Finance is, "Don't you understand that we take some of those funds and we distribute them among provincial governments?" If the federal government distributes them among provincial governments it is because of a national policy. It is no answer to say the money goes elsewhere. The money is, in fact, collected and then it is disbursed in a fashion which the federal government desires. It is its responsibility to account for its constant groping for tax dollars resulting from the hard work and efforts of Canadians.
Where has all this led us? It has led us from the time the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office to a government spending program which has grown from some SI2 billion to some $66.6 billion. It has resulted in an interest element on the national debt of $12.26 billion, or almost equal to the entire budgetary estimates of the Prime Minister who is now in office, when he came to office-almost an equivalent amount is now spent paying interest on the national debt. But, Mr. Speaker, even these figures are wrong. We learned from the deputy minister of finance last week that the Canada pension fund is fully $102 billion unfunded. The plan would be insolvent if it were called upon to meet the obligations it has to Canadians who have looked upon the Canada Pension Plan as a contract between themselves and the Government of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the $66.6 billion to which I have made reference does not include-

Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting to hear members opposite complaining about the amount of government expenditures. I have been here almost 13 years-I was not here during the 1979-1980 regime-and I have yet to hear a recommendation from members opposite about areas in which the government should be cutting its expenditures. This was very much in evidence when the official opposition formed the government. I did not see too many significant cuts but I saw significant increases in
June 26, 1981

expenditures. Fortunately this House saw fit to defeat that budget, otherwise we would have been in dire straits and possibly in the economic crisis which the opposition alleges is taking place today.
In my position as Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, I would be remiss if I did not publicly compliment the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), who is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres). In a short period we have had the Bank Act, which is a massive piece of legislation, and Bill C-57 before the finance committee. Whatever your views were on either one of those pieces of legislation, Mr. Speaker, they called for a great deal of homework, study and understanding. The parliamentary secretary made a point of briefing himself so that he could intelligently cope with the matter as a member of that committee, but he has been given the significant tribute today of handling this debate on behalf of the government in a motion raised by the opposition. I compliment him for the work he has performed.
We hear about an economic crisis. I do not think the people who raise that kind of issue have talked to the people at FIRA. The Foreign Investment Review Agency has never received more applications, or had more people from outside of this country endeavouring to invest in Canada because they realize it is an excellent place to invest. We can keep our interest rates below those of the United States because we are a country where people are not afraid to invest their money. As a matter of fact, every day people are seeking ways to buy, to invest or to start up new industries.
Sell out the whole country.

The economy could not be in crisis if that were the situation. I hear hon. members opposite saying "tell that to the farmers" or "tell that to the small businessman". Anyone who talks about the economy being in crisis is really doing a disservice to the small businessman and to the farmer. It is as though we were going to hell in a hand basket, if you listen to members opposite.
The facts have been spelled out in statistics. Fortunately for the government and for Canada we have a very sophisticated group of Canadians who understand that all the faults and all the problems we have cannot be placed on the government's doorstep.
1 agree with the hon. member who preceded me in one area, that it is to the government's credit to have cut back the monetary supply. I agree with him that earlier we had expanded the money supply and risked some inflation in the interests of keeping jobs in the economy. It was a trade-off at that time. If we had cut back on the money supply instead of increasing it, we would have faced a much more serious problem of very high unemployment, in the late 1960s and the early 1970s. The government took the conscious decision. It is all well and good to say in hindsight that it was wrong to increase the money supply at that time, but they were not prepared to face the
Economic Policies
problems that Canada would have had with hundreds of thousands more unemployed. Therefore it was a conscious, legitimate, bona fide decision in the interests of saving jobs. Had we not had the quadrupling of the oil prices, I suggest with respect, that move would have been complimented and not criticized at the present time.
I hear members opposite saying that we could solve all the problems in Canada if we could just get the energy situation, the pricing and the distribution of the money settled. But I was surprised to hear a member from Alberta suggesting the other day that we could solve all our problems immediately by going to 75 per cent of world price. First, it is irresponsible to suggest that we should tie our prices to a world price when we have seen OPEC quadruple the price of oil overnight. Who is to say that OPEC will not double it overnight at some stage? Why should we tie our price to the world price? Second, by going overnight to 75 per cent of world price, can you imagine the impact on provinces like Quebec and the four Atlantic provinces, just to name those provinces that would have more difficulty coping with that particular sudden rise? I suggest that all of Canada would suffer if we moved in a precipitous way to that price.
We all know that the price of oil is too low at the present time. We all know that the price has to rise. But surely common sense dictates that we must find a procedure whereby we can augment this cost of oil and do it in a careful, appropriate and sensible way. We must not say that all our problems will go away if we yield to what the oil producers are saying, particularly the oil producing provinces, and go to 75 per cent of world price overnight. That will not resolve anything.
What I do welcome are those suggestions coming to me from my riding. As Chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, I get other suggestions from across Canada. One suggestion came from a constituent who suggested that the government give consideration to tax exempt bonds. In this way an individual could earn a certain amount of interest, say 50 per cent of the going rate, and that money could then be loaned out to help small industries. This would be another source of revenue. That suggestion has been criticized because it would be beneficial only to those who have money and there are other avenues whereby they could get tax advantages. But, of course, if you are going to get money, you are going to get it from the people who have it, those who are prepared to buy these bonds knowing that they will be tax exempt. It would be of significant benefit to Canadians and to farmers if the money were used in that particular way.
When are you going to bring in that provision?
I have made about four or five suggestions to the Minister of Finance.
He hasn't taken any notice.

Whether he sees fit to adopt all or any of them, we will have to wait for the October budget. I think we do a disservice if we are afraid or do not stand up to be counted in

June 26, 1981
Economic Policies
areas where we think moves should be made by the Department of Finance. Political palliatives that we hear from members of the opposition will not do the trick. They are talking about mortgage protection. Members of the NDP are talking about a modified form of exchange controls, but they are very careful not to spell that out. They talk about freezing interest rates but not having to accept the responsibility of what would happen to the Canadian dollar. Senator Lamontagne said the other day that the value of the Canadian dollar in terms of the U.S. dollar might go down to 78 cents. He has no guarantee that will happen. 1 suggest, with respect, that he is way off base on that suggestion.
I understand I am allowed 20 minutes in this debate, but in the interests of allowing one of my friends opposite to participate, 1 will cut my remarks short. I had other things 1 wanted to say, but I will only mention one. I watched television last night and I was appalled that the banks have indicated to the Minister of Finance that they are prepared to "bend over backward" to help out industry or to help out the small businessman. A bank has decided to move in on a business run by three generations of one family in Bridgeport, Nova Scotia after having been told by the family that they needed two or three more weeks in order to succeed. When banks do not play their part in an area such as that, they are doing a disservice to their customers which they have been pleased and proud to have in the past. When businesses like that get into difficulty and the banks have to make a move, it should be a move in the right direction, which is to help their customers as every other business is required to do at the present. But if banks move in this way they are not, in my view, meeting their social obligations.
There are other areas on which I want to comment but I have agreed to give some of my time so that other members have the opportunity to speak.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member who has just concluded his remarks and allowed me to speak this afternoon. I am pleased to speak on the motion presented by the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Gurbin) concerning the economic crisis in this country brought on by the government's handling of interest rates. We do not always look at the question of interest rates as widely as we might. I do not intend to spend a lot of time in my remarks dealing with the why of interest rates. However, I want to deal with the two basic answers we usually hear from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) as to why we have high interest rates.
Sometimes he says it is to attract money to this country. That sounds reasonable. At the same time members of the official opposition say that too much money has been manufactured in this country. When we look at the assets of the banks in this country we see that in 1970 they had approximately $32 billion in assets to loan. In 1980 this had increased to $340 billion. The amount of money that is available beyond
the direct control of government has grown at a phenomenal rate.
We had the Bank Act before us within the last year. The amount of reserves that the banks are forced to keep were reduced. That results in the amount of money which they can loan for every dollar invested with them increasing that much quicker. Therefore, we have not done very much with regard to regulating the banks. We have virtually allowed the interest rate to be set by an auction every week. I am not certain it has had the desired result.
Our finance critic pointed out that Statistics Canada reports show that consumers and small businessmen have reduced their spending between 40 and 60 per cent. Therefore, they are not bidding up the price for goods and services. They are reducing their spending. However, interest rates keep going up, ostensibly to force us to reduce spending. I do not know where the vicious cycle will end. I know it is affecting farmers in particular, and it is my responsibility to speak for them in this House on behalf of our caucus.
I wish to spend a few minutes to make the House aware of some of the difficulties that have been created for farmers and small businesses. There are a number of cases I could deal with, but I will review two with the House. These are not beginning farmers, poor operators or poor managers. They have grown very rapidly in their first 10 or 20 years in the business and were at a level of production that is considered to be an economic unit, yet both are in trouble.
Case number one is a Saskatchewan farmer who added a half section of land to a section and a half that he was farming just three years ago. The half section which he added cost him $130,000, all of which he borrowed. That was and still is the only debt he has. However, he had a three year renegotiable mortgage and the three years are now up. His interest payments will double from $16,000 to $32,000 per year. The extra increase in interest payments that are due each year equal or exceed his net income for the previous year.
This man is 43 years old, is operating what is considered to be an economic unit, has a good turnover, fairly good grain prices and is considering selling out. That is because the increase in interest rates will virtually wipe out his net income. If he offers the land for sale, the amount of money he will have to reinvest at today's interest rates will easily give him a net income of $60,000 a year before taxes, and possibly more than that. For doing absolutely nothing, he will triple his income. Another relatively young farmer will be going out of business.
The other case involves a tobacco farmer in Ontario who is ten years younger, in his early thirties. He has had two difficult years. His tobacco crop was damaged by frost and disease during the last two years. It reduced his income by about 20 per cent in each of those two years. As a result, his debt load has been increasing.
This man sent me his financial statement for the two years. For the year ending April 30, 1980, his interest payments amounted to $26,934. For the year ended April 30, 1981, carrying very little more debt, they totalled $58,163. He has
June 26, 1981

attempted to reincorporate his farm to be eligible for a small business development bond. However, he may not be eligible. Going to SBDB would bring the interest load down $18,000 or $20,000, which would allow him and his wife some money to spend.
These are the kinds of situation that farmers are getting into. Many farmers have to re-mortgage their land because mortgage rates are usually slightly lower than operating loans. It is reminiscent of the old Woodie Guthrie song which went like this:
The mortgage worked the steadiest and the hardest of us all.
It worked all week and Sundays, it worked each holiday,
It settled down among us and never went away.
Indeed, mortgages on farm land are not going away. Debt on the farm is increasing much faster on an annual basis than almost any segment of our economy. The economic analysis being done by the finance minister perhaps identifies some of the problems in this country. When the finance minister was studying and indeed teaching economics, the country was considered to have three sectors to its economy. In the fifties, the primary production sector made up 30 per cent of the economy, the manufacturing sector 30 per cent and the service sector 40 per cent. To some extent, our monetary and fiscal policies still seem to run with those basic concepts of the economy.
Unfortunately, the situation has changed considerably. Our primary production now employs about 7.6 per cent of all those employed in this country, that is agriculture, forestry and fisheries. The manufacturing sector which processes the goods and manufactures the tools and equipment accounts for about 25 per cent of our employment. The service sector in today's economy accounts for well over two-thirds of our employment, or 67.4 per cent. When we look at the new situation, we see that the old solutions will not work. In the old days, with the old economics, the agricultural sector was considered to have too much labour. We are always told that we are underutilizing our labour, that we have far too much of it and all of the policies are aimed at getting people out of agriculture. I think nearly all agricultural economists have been of the opinion for the last five or ten years that, if anything, there is a shortage of real skilled labour in agriculture. When we see people like the young tobacco farmer or the grain farmer in Saskatchewan being forced out of agriculture, or coaxed out, by the kind of interest rate policies we have, we realize we are losing a very unique and important part of the economy of this country.
Seven or eight years ago there was a study done which indicated that in terms of the gross national product agriculture was responsible for producing or contributing something like 42 per cent. That may have changed a little in intervening years, but it is still a very sizeable amount. Even though it does not employ very many people, it is still responsible for providing goods that can be used in manufacture and for providing
Economic Policies
services to the point that a great number of people still rely on it in this economy.
Although the policy of high interest rates under old economics might not bother the government very much, the fact that we are losing some farmers is going to have a disastrous effect. I would cite some of the reactions that some of the farmers in my part of the country are indicating when talking of high interest rates. Many of them are mixed farmers producing hogs and beef.
There is a man in the Rosthern area, for instance, whose father and grandfather have produced registered hogs since the opening up of that part of the country. He is considering shutting down his farm, which will mean about 2,000 pigs per year out of production. Not only will this take hogs out of production, it will do away with a number of fairly important breed or genetic lines which have been introduced into the livestock business. He is doing this for a very simple and fundamental reason. By selling off his livestock, he will have a bit more money to reduce his debt load, thus reducing the amount of interest payable.
What happens one or two years down the road when he no longer has these 2,000 pigs from his farm coming into the economy? What impact will the consumers feel? We have seen an Economic Council report complaining about marketing boards and how they are costly to consumers, but what happens in this free market system when we put people out of production and we do not have that production for consumers to consume? How is that going to fail to be anything but costly to consumers?
We think there has to be a better way of handling the economy. We think interest rates to farmers should be reduced. We have offered in this House and to the minister in committee a number of proposals to increase the use of Farm Credit Corporation loans. We have outlined ways of increasing the amount of money available to the Farm Credit Corporation without having to come to Parliament and without having to increase government allocation. There are many people who are selling farms who would reinvest that money in corporation bonds if there was a tax provision allowing it. We think there are a number of things that can be done.
I see my time is up, Mr. Speaker, but I would again reiterate that high interest rates are killing the people on the farms, small businessmen and home owners, and something should be done about it.
